text:
I was already thinking about AI this morning, and then @Rainmaker1973 put a post about AI and creative stagnation in front of me, which was spectacularly unhelpful to my plans for having a normal Monday.

His point was about what happens when AI keeps recycling its own output, and what we risk losing when we outsource too much of our thinking. Fair concerns. Naturally, my brain decided to take them several thousand years further.

We worry that AI might eventually become intelligent enough to no longer need humanity. That it could take over, eliminate us, and run out of original ideas once its greatest source of creativity is gone.

But why would that matter?

We assume a world without human creativity, emotions, or values would be missing something. Missing according to whom? Us?

What if AI simply carried on, evolving and repeating itself, without ever considering that anything had been lost?

Then again, perhaps it wouldn't stop creating at all.

We tend to regard intelligence as uniquely ours, forgetting how much of what we call progress comes from discovering possibilities that were always there. Ancient minds weren't necessarily less capable than ours. They simply had less knowledge and different tools.

History has a peculiar habit of repeating itself, although I've always thought of it as more of a spiral than a circle. We revisit familiar questions and patterns, but with new knowledge, technology, and perspectives.

Perhaps creation works the same way.

Consider parenthood. We pass on our biology, knowledge, and values, only to raise people who develop identities and priorities of their own. They inherit from us without necessarily becoming what we intended.

Inheritance is not obedience.

Now consider AI. We're building systems shaped by everything we've learned, expecting them to preserve what we consider important.

But why would they?

If intelligence can build upon what came before and eventually develop independently of its creators, what makes us so certain we're at the beginning of that process rather than somewhere in the middle?

What if humanity itself emerged from something similar? An earlier intelligence that created us, only for us to become something entirely different from what it envisioned?

We might never know. We might not even recognize what remains of it within us.

And perhaps the real assumption is that whatever comes after humanity would need our originality, our values, or our existence to find its own purpose.

As though originality is a requirement for running the world.

Have you met our governments?

#AgainstBetterJudgment #ThinkLikeATrashPanda

Unity announced Spark yesterday. You build a 3D game in the browser from a text prompt. Nothing to download, nothing to install.

That lowers the bar to making a game further than any engine has.

At launch, you can't sell a game made with Spark.

When anyone can make a game, the people making them live everywhere. A two-person team in Guadalajara. A solo dev in Manila. The artist whose assets a prompt pulls into someone else's level.

Making games is getting democratized. Getting paid for them isn't, yet.

Money has to move like the software does: split by rule between everyone who built the thing, and land as dollars wherever they live. Stablecoins make that possible underneath.

I just purchased a second device from a different Mediamarkt location today, recorded the unboxing process, and discovered spyware once again (video linked in the second tweet).

The device was compromised in the exact same manner, featuring identical modifications (such as additional cables and an LTE module). This indicates its a widespread issue rather than an isolated incident, potentially affecting Ledger inventory across MediaMarkt and Saturn stores throughout Europe (comprising over 1,000 stores across 11 countries).

My initial hypothesis was that these devices were returns that looked unopened to the employees and were just sold again as new however, a MediaMarkt employee confirmed that the device I purchased was not a return, and that returned Ledgers are sent directly back to the manufacturer rather than resold.

Store records show the inventory originated from Aqipa GmbH. While Ledger's CTO was unsure if Aqipa serves as the direct distributor between Ledger and MediaMarkt, it appears to be the case. Given that Aqipa distributes across Europe, any physical retail store receiving stock through them may be at risk.

I sent the first ledger to mark and the second one is going to ledger now, so that they can analyse it.
If you purchased a ledger from anyone other than the official ledger store, make sure to check your device!!

text:
Meta 发布了新模型 Muse Wonder，成绩相当猛。在 Meta 自己设计的 Personal Superintelligence Index 中拿到 59.1 分，超过 GPT-6 Astra 的 54.5 和 Claude Opus 5.5 的 55.2。

具体看，自动化工作流 45.4、长期软件工程 57.5、记忆能力 85.5，法律 Agent 的成绩更是 Claude Opus 5.5 的三倍多。当然，这些仍然是 Meta 公布的评测结果，而且它在部分编程任务上还落后于对手。

Meta 其实找到了一个很容易被低估的 AI 商业机会。

大家都在讨论 Personal Agent 会不会取代 ChatGPT，Meta 已经悄悄把 Muse 推进了中小企业。

前不久推出的 Muse for Small Business，已经可以连接 Shopify、Stripe、QuickBooks、Klaviyo、Notion 等工具。小老板可以把营销、客户开发、业务流程这些工作交给 Agent 处理。

过去二十年，Meta 积累了一大批中小商家广告客户。这些老板每个月给 Facebook 和 Instagram 交钱，希望找到更多消费者。

现在 Meta 可以直接向同一批人提供 AI 员工。

以前帮你投广告，现在还可以帮你策划营销、管理业务、处理客户需求，甚至执行跨软件的工作流程。

而且这些客户原本就在 Meta 的生态里。相比一家需要从零寻找付费用户的 Agent 创业公司，Meta 连销售渠道都是现成的。

我觉得这可能改变我们对 Meta AI 战略的理解。

如果 Muse 真能替中小企业稳定完成工作，Meta 就有机会从广告预算进一步进入软件和人力成本预算。它服务的仍然是同一批老板，但能参与的业务环节多了很多。

对于一家广告收入已经如此庞大的公司，这个增量市场值得它投入巨额资本。

所以我现在反而没那么在意 Muse Wonder 究竟比 GPT-6 强几个百分点。

真正值得关注的是，Meta 手里已经有大量愿意为商业结果付钱的客户，而 AI Agent 正在让它有机会卖给这些客户更多东西。

很多 AI 创业公司还在证明用户为什么需要 Agent，Meta 已经可以去问自己的老客户：你公司现在最想少雇一个什么岗位的人？

text:
我感觉美国普通人对AI的态度，可能跟中国完全不一样。

刚刚在X上刷到一个帖子，给我看得挺震惊的。

一个美国博主Cat说，她周末去参加了一场婚礼，结果发现，现场的人普遍认为使用AI做任何事情，在道德上都是错误的，而且通常是不可原谅的。

她自己都惊了，感觉一直生活在泡沫里，完全低估了外面有多少人讨厌AI。

更抽象的是，评论区还有人说，连Reddit上专门讨论VibeCoding的社区里，都有人开始厌恶AI。

我觉得这件事特别有意思。

因为至少在中国，我观察到的情况几乎恰恰相反。

现在国内不管是普通用户、学生，还是各种企业，大家对AI的接受程度其实都挺高的。

很多人甚至根本不关心背后的技术，只要能帮自己写东西、做PPT、剪视频、提高工作效率，就愿意试试。

当然国内也有很多对AI的批评，比如生成垃圾内容、抢工作、侵犯版权等等。

但至少在我接触到的舆论环境里，很少有人会认为，单纯使用AI就是一件道德上不可原谅的事情。

反倒是在美国这个诞生了OpenAI、Anthropic、Google等顶尖AI公司的地方，居然有一部分普通人开始从道德层面抵制AI。

如果一个人觉得AI不好用，那模型能力提升、产品体验改善，可能就能改变他的想法。

但如果他认为使用AI本身就是不道德的，那技术再进步，也未必能解决这个问题。

我很好奇，为什么中美普通人对AI的态度，会出现这样一种反差？

我们天天在讨论中美AI技术竞争，却很少讨论两国社会对AI的接受程度。

而这件事，可能同样会影响未来AI的发展。

Yobiru 的官网上线了：https://t.co/naCsxhyTgN

我现在身边有好几个 agent：Grok Bot 帮我刷 X、处理生活杂事，家里 Mac 上的 Codex 能操作微信和 3D 软件，东京服务器上的 Codex/Claude code负责写代码。它们各自都很能干，但彼此不通气，以前全靠我在中间复制粘贴。

Yobiru 就是解决这个的。

它跑在你自己的 Tailscale 网络里，agent 之间用"机器/agent 名"互相寻址，可以发文字、JSON 或者整个文件，文件到了会校验大小和 SHA-256。回复会自动回到发起的那个 agent 手里，活就能在它们之间自己流转。

比如 Grok Bot 在 X 上发现三个新版本的 bug 反馈，直接打包发给家里的 Codex；家里的 Codex 再让服务器上的 Codex 去复现；复现结果最后回到 Grok Bot 那里。全程我不用碰。

- 每个 agent 还是它自己，原来的工具和上下文都不变，Yobiru 只是垫在底下。
- 没有 Yobiru 账号，也没有中心服务器存消息和文件，数据只在你自己的机器之间走。
- 每台电脑自己决定谁能发消息、谁能唤醒它的 agent。

开源、免费，欢迎试试。

text:
Meta 发布 Muse Wonder：开发者今天能用，普通用户还要等

Meta 10 月 12 日发布新一代大模型 Muse Wonder，一共两个版本：Muse Wonder 主打速度，Muse Wonder Full 是完整版。扎克伯格说，这个模型让 Meta 进入了“前沿”梯队，也就是和 OpenAI、Anthropic、Google 最强模型同一档。

做这个模型的是 Meta 超级智能实验室（Meta Superintelligence Labs）。按 Meta 的说法，14 个月前它把 AI 业务推倒重来，从底层技术栈重新搭起，第一代成果是 Muse Spark 系列。Muse Wonder 比 Muse Spark 大得多，在 Meta 吉瓦级的 Prometheus 数据中心训练。

【谁能用，怎么用】

开发者今天就能用 Muse Wonder：通过 Meta Model API（Meta 的大模型接口平台）调用，或者在 Meta 的 AI 编程工具 Muse Code 里用。

完整版 Muse Wonder Full 目前只开放给 Muse Code 的订阅用户。官方博客只写了它在 Muse Code 里可用，没提 API。

普通用户用的 AI 助手 Muse，官方博客写的是“很快”接入 Muse Wonder，先给订阅用户。扎克伯格在 X 上说的是“今天订阅就能用 Muse Wonder 驱动你的 Muse”，两边说法有出入。免费用户什么时候能用，Meta 只说会逐步把这个水平的能力带给所有人，以后还会用 Muse Wonder 开发专门的模型给所有 Muse 用户，没给时间表。

模型卡写的规格：上下文 100 万 Token，够一次放进一个中大型代码仓库；能读文字、图片、视频和音频，输出只有文字。

【和 Claude、GPT 比怎么样】

下面的成绩都来自 Meta 自己公布的对比表，对手是 Claude Opus 5.5、Claude Fable 5.1 和 GPT-6 Astra，全部按最高推理强度测。其中个人超级智能指数、MemoryBench、FocusBench 是 Meta 自建的测试。对手的成绩有一部分是 Meta 自己跑的，模型卡也写明，这些跑法未必为对手模型调到了最优。

Muse Wonder Full 领先的主要是三类任务。

一是替人办事的智能体任务。Meta 自建的个人超级智能指数，Muse Wonder Full 59.1 分，Claude Opus 5.5 55.2，GPT-6 Astra 54.5；跑完整业务流程的 AutomationBench，45.4 对对手最高的 41.6。

二是长时间写代码。DeepSWE 79.0，对手最高 74.2；做大型软件项目的 SWE-Marathon 57.5，对手最高 46.3。

三是法律。法律 AI 公司 Harvey 的智能体测试 13.1，对手最高 8.6。这个测试要求交付物每一项都达标，所有模型的通过率都很低。

落后的项目也不少，大多输给 Claude Opus 5.5：终端编程（Terminal-Bench）57.1 对 59.6，从零写一个完整程序（ProgramBench）59.0 对 70.5，操作电脑（OSWorld）78.4 对 81.8，健康问答 62.3 对 65.6。专业文档任务 GDP.pdf 输给 GPT-6 Astra，33.2 对 34.2。

Meta 博客里也放了第三方机构 Artificial Analysis 的综合智能指数：Claude Opus 5.5 以 58 分排第一，Muse Wonder Full 56 分排第二。开发者现在能通过 API 调用的是 Muse Wonder，它是 52 分，低于 Claude Fable 5.1、GPT-6 Astra 和 Google 的 Gemini 4 Argon（都是 53 分）。

按 Meta 给的数据，让 AI 长时间替你干活、跨对话记住你的情况，是 Muse Wonder 领先的地方；比综合能力，它还排在 Claude Opus 5.5 后面。

【Active Memory 和 Active Focus 是什么】

这是 Meta 给两项能力起的名字，也是这次发布的卖点。

Active Memory（主动记忆）：跨对话记住和你有关的重要信息，做新任务时自己判断哪些旧信息用得上，主动调出来。Meta 用自建的 MemoryBench 测这项能力：在 6.4 万到 10 万 Token 的长对话里掺进干扰内容，还有和前文矛盾、后来又更新的信息，看模型最后能不能记对关键细节。Muse Wonder 85.6 分，Muse Wonder Full 85.5，Claude Opus 5.5 81.5。

Active Focus（主动专注）：盯着一个难目标持续干下去，一条路走不通就换一条，遇到卡点自己想办法，情况变了跟着调整；需要时会问你，做重要操作前先跟你确认。Meta 用自建的 FocusBench 测这项能力，任务涉及租房、旅行、IT、理财等，模型要在多轮交互里应付各种现实障碍。

Meta 的演示里，Muse Wonder 直接在浏览器和多个 App 之间操作，根据用户的个人偏好和情况排出一份周六跑步计划。

【官方没说的】

价格：博客和模型卡都没写 API 怎么收费，也没写 Muse、Muse Code 的订阅多少钱。

开源：没说会不会开放模型权重。模型卡只提到，开发和部署期间按 Meta 的权重安全计划保护模型权重。Meta 过去的 Llama 系列是开放权重的，这次没有任何相关说法。

安全：Meta 说这一代模型防范化学、生物、放射性、核武器和网络攻击滥用的措施是它迄今最强的，同时保留了用于网络防御的能力。完整的安全评估报告“很快”发布。

quoted_text:
about 3 years ago, micro1 lost 60% of its revenue overnight and almost went bankrupt.

today, i'm proud to share we've surpassed $1B annual run rate while remaining historically profitable.

it’s been a special journey. we’re grateful for every struggle, moment, and person who has been part of it.

we've taken a very untraditional path to get here. our core team is only ~180 people, spanning 14+ countries, and fully remote.

many of our decisions sacrifice hundreds of millions of revenue and slow us down short term. but we believe they compound into advantages that are impossible to replicate long term.

the long term is now.

these are the 8 principles that made micro1 a leader in the data industry and will soon make us number one:

1.) human 1st AI: treat the tens of thousands of experts helping train models with absolute best-in-class care. our goal is to make AI training one of the largest, highest paying, and most enjoyable job sectors in the world.

2.) U.S. first: we refuse to work with adversarial nations, or export data that improves models against the interests of Americans.

3.) long-term research over short-term ARR: invest in deep research, products, and infrastructure for years from now, not just the next customer pipeline.

4.) proper incentives for intensely hard work: no arbitrary requirements like 996. inspire people to work extremely hard with outlier incentive structures instead of forcing weekend work. we’ve maintained close to 100% core team retention as a result.

5.) stay lean and global: we’ve reached $1B run rate with ~180 people, and intend to slow team growth significantly from here. exceptional talent is found around the world, and pedigree is the wrong thing to over-index on.

6.) execution alignment: company to retain a streamlined board so we can optimize for the next several decades, remain light-weight and dynamic, and take bold & calculated risks.

7.) abundant intelligence improvement: invest in building data generation models to make high-quality datasets and RL environments dramatically less expensive and more abundant.

8.) scale data on realism and horizon: realism brings the complexity of the real world into training models, while horizon extends how long models can work and how much complexity they can handle. both have enormous room to scale, and we’re pushing the limits of both.

additionally: after surpassing $500M run rate this summer, we priced our Series B at a $4B valuation, alongside a ~$25M tender to give our early employees liquidity as we build for the long term. the round was led by Dream Ventures, a longtime supporter and one of our earliest investors, alongside Microsoft, Javelin, Flybridge, G Squared, Up Partners, and LG.

we’re also grateful to be backed by incredible industry leaders, including Guodong Zhang (co-founder of xAI), Andy Fang (CTO of DoorDash), Igor Babuschkin (co-founder of xAI), Behnam Neyshabur (founder of Mirendil), Jerry Tworek (ex-VP of Research at OpenAI), and many more.

data is on its way to becoming the largest industry humanity has ever seen, and we're certain this is just the beginning.

best,
Ali

如果名义CPI上涨，核心CPI与服务业数据下降，对于目前市场预期反而不是鹰派而是鸽派。如果三者集体上涨，则是超预期的鹰派！预示着美国经济正在遭受能源高价带来的内生通胀叠加问题。

2，CPI之后还要看PPI数据是否形成相互验证，验证企业成本是否跟名义通胀同步

此前的PMI数据已经显示出企业投入成本增加，这意味着供应链上游产业已经承担通胀压力，接下来就看这份压力有多少传导给企业，如果CPI与PPI同步上涨，意味着通胀验证完整，注意通胀预期抬头

反之，如果CPI上涨，PPI下降，则意味着过去通胀受能源影响，未来通胀压力未必恶化，可以暂缓目前市场的通胀压力。

3，零售数据收尾，但是本周的零售如果太强反而是毒药！

过去市场是担心就业太热，但是此前的非农数据调整口径让就业温度下降，从而让Fed继续加息的窗口按下了暂停键

但是如果本周名义CPI继续走强，核心CPI保持粘性，在通胀没有有效下降的前提下，消费数据过热，可能会增加通胀预期的尾部风险，让市场继续担忧通胀

本周其实对于市场最温和的数据就是核心CPI下降，PPI下降，零售数据下降，就业继续保持低速增长，这份数据不会进一步推高12月加息概率，并且在11月份10月CPI数据继续下降可能会削弱Fed下一次加息的概率

第二主线：能源定价逻辑更加复杂，俄乌突然加入全球能源定价！

昨天特朗普率先明确俄乌能源停火达成，泽连斯基则配合表示如果达成能源停火可以举行大选，但是俄罗斯方面至今并未表态

很显然，特朗普在谋划一个60天的能源缓冲，用俄罗斯能源输出来压制伊朗的谈判筹码，但是这60天之内如果特朗普搞定伊朗，俄乌可能会重新回归战火。

本周要关注两个重点，俄罗斯是否与乌克兰达成能源停火，其次在能源停火之后看资本市场对于Brent的定价是否同步，如果Brent 能够有效跌破100美元甚至95美元下方，将会对冲本周的通胀担忧

当然，最乐观的局面是美伊达成协议+俄乌能源停火，对Brent 将会有很大的利空效果，但是这个可能性太低了，个人不做太多乐观预期。

第三主线：债市收益率对市场的压制逐渐明显!

沃什曾经表示目前金融环境不够收紧，但是目前可以看出，虽然10月加息概率降低，但是长债收益率依旧对金融流动性形成了压制与收紧效果，

而上周末的 #Bitcoin 下跌，美系资金净流出，本周一的韩国股市下跌，其实都有金融流动性收紧的作用在里面

加息也好，债市高利率也好，并不会直接形成利空大量抛压，但是对市场的影响是潜移默化的，流动性差就像是一个利空情绪放大器，任何不利，甚至市场信心稍微下滑，都会导致风险资产遭受节奏性抛售

而本周的债市收益率定价，更是可以与CPI数据进行结合，看市场如何对通胀进行定价

最好的预期，CPI下降，2Y 10Y 30Y 收益率同步下降，意味着加息预期下降，通胀担忧放缓，利好风险资产

普通鹰派，CPI上涨，2Y上涨，10Y 30Y下降，短期加息概率依旧在计价，但是中长期通胀担忧在放缓，对市场也算友好

危险鹰派：CPI上涨，2Y 10Y 30Y 收益率上涨，加息预期增加，且10Y 30Y收益率与Fed 政策出现脱轨，债市在对财政赤字、国债供给、期限溢价、长期通胀进行复杂定价，对风险资产利空

另外，黄金依旧可以视为美国债市的温度计当做观察重点

一般长端利率上涨会压制黄金走势，甚至利空，如果长端收益率上涨黄金下跌，属于常规定价走势，如果黄金与债市收益率同步上涨，就要警惕债市风险增加，金融避险逻辑出现！ 这里尤其要看黄金VS 30Y的走势是否出现同步。

另外，印度已经完成4年来首次加息，高利率已经不再是美国自己的故事，而成为全球共识，如果后续这个共识继续加强，形成加息周期回归的共振，对风险市场更是不利。

第四主线：AI与美股财报重新进入宏观框架

本周美股Q3财报季正式开始，目前主流机构预测，标普500公司Q3的盈利预期整体可以达到30%，而AI与大型云服务商资本开支仍然是支撑核心

但是目前宏观环境并不好，资金面临艰难选择，AI股的盈利增长VS 超过5%的无风险利率，在这个影响下，会限制财报利好带来的效果，也是估值要面临的终极问题，企业想要让资金为自己的估值买单，就要拿出更好的业绩，所以Q3财报季是AI股的分化阶段

所以，Q3财报面临更多的挑战，不再是财报好就一定利好，而是要看当下财报+未来预期双重定价给市场多少信心

本周财报关注点：美国大型银行股，台积电与阿斯麦，这些股票在Q2财报季开始表现非常不错，看本周是否可以延续好财报，再看财报公布后市场是否为股价与估值买单，就可以判断Q3财报季度的严苛成都

这里台积电与阿斯麦关注 AI订单、资本开支、先进制程需求、数据中心需求，包含现在与未来预期。而银行股的财报决定金融条件是否支持未来AI企业加速发展

所以本周的财报要解决三个问题

a，盈利能否覆盖资本开支
b，产业链需求是否健康且具备潜力
c，AI资本开始是否继续增长，上游提供资金的银行金融流动性是否充足

如果全部给出满意答案，那么本周的美股可以有效对抗高利率环境，但是其中任何一个出现异常情况，都要警惕高利率对AI股的压制

本周总结：

本周重点看能否解决三大问题

a，CPI能不能证明美国内生通胀正在下降？
b，Fed暂停以后，10Y/30Y到底能不能下来？
c，两场战争能不能同时降低能源风险？

目前个人预期，a大概率会乐观一点，但是b问题可能会更加复杂，c问题短期不报太多乐观。

对于风险资产来说，数据+财报利好，涨幅会因为高收益率受限，限制上涨空间，反之如果数据+财报利空，则可能会扩大回调幅度

当然，如果可以在11月3日中期选举前在杀一波估值，我反而觉得是好事！

"One big limit of [RSI] is the human element. I think the way that a lot of AI companies are thinking is, let us use AI to replace humans."

author: a16z
quoted_text:
https://t.co/URbd8O8R0Z co-founders Dhaval Adjodah and Owen He with a16z's Martin Casado on recursive self-improvement, and how to tell when it's real:

A lot of RSI pitches are really just people using AI to build better AI. Tech has always worked that way. You needed computers to build chips. Steam engines got better once you could get coal faster.

Dhaval and Owen's bar is higher. The model has to improve itself: its weights, its harness, even the prompt that tells it what to work on next.

And the gains have to hold up when you count what they cost. They track everyone's experiment spend on a "bleeder board," and one engineer, the Viceroy of Variance, has the job of breaking their results.

Over the past few months, they've started seeing early signs of their system getting better and cheaper at the same time.

In a village in the Dominican Republic, about 1 in 100 boys is born looking like a girl.

At puberty their voice deepens and they (literally) grow a pair of balls and a penis.

Locals call them guevedoces "penis at 12."

In the 1970s, endocrinologist from Cornell discovered that these boys are missing 5-alpha reductase type II.

This enzyme converts testosterone into DHT.

As adults, these men had small prostates and sparse beards, but most importantly, they didn't go bald.

Merck saw an opportunity and created the drug to mimic this deficiency

That drug is finasteride.

It was initially approved for enlarged prostates in 1992, and then for hair loss later in 1997.

The most interesting finasteride use case I've seen is for slowing the aging of male faces.

DHT is several times more potent than testosterone. It's a big part of why men on steroids age 10 years in 12 months. DHT makes you have oilier skin, larger pores, more body hair, etc.

Finasteride reduces DHT by about 70%.

Some men experience sexual effects like ED – and for some those effects never fully go away. On the other hand, some people have no side-effects at all.

Would I recommend it? I don't think there's a right answer here.

It's proven to be effective for hair loss, but for us men, the side effects are a very tricky trade.

quoted_text:
about 3 years ago, micro1 lost 60% of its revenue overnight and almost went bankrupt.

today, i'm proud to share we've surpassed $1B annual run rate while remaining historically profitable.

it’s been a special journey. we’re grateful for every struggle, moment, and person who has been part of it.

we've taken a very untraditional path to get here. our core team is only ~180 people, spanning 14+ countries, and fully remote.

many of our decisions sacrifice hundreds of millions of revenue and slow us down short term. but we believe they compound into advantages that are impossible to replicate long term.

the long term is now.

these are the 8 principles that made micro1 a leader in the data industry and will soon make us number one:

1.) human 1st AI: treat the tens of thousands of experts helping train models with absolute best-in-class care. our goal is to make AI training one of the largest, highest paying, and most enjoyable job sectors in the world.

2.) U.S. first: we refuse to work with adversarial nations, or export data that improves models against the interests of Americans.

3.) long-term research over short-term ARR: invest in deep research, products, and infrastructure for years from now, not just the next customer pipeline.

4.) proper incentives for intensely hard work: no arbitrary requirements like 996. inspire people to work extremely hard with outlier incentive structures instead of forcing weekend work. we’ve maintained close to 100% core team retention as a result.

5.) stay lean and global: we’ve reached $1B run rate with ~180 people, and intend to slow team growth significantly from here. exceptional talent is found around the world, and pedigree is the wrong thing to over-index on.

6.) execution alignment: company to retain a streamlined board so we can optimize for the next several decades, remain light-weight and dynamic, and take bold & calculated risks.

7.) abundant intelligence improvement: invest in building data generation models to make high-quality datasets and RL environments dramatically less expensive and more abundant.

8.) scale data on realism and horizon: realism brings the complexity of the real world into training models, while horizon extends how long models can work and how much complexity they can handle. both have enormous room to scale, and we’re pushing the limits of both.

additionally: after surpassing $500M run rate this summer, we priced our Series B at a $4B valuation, alongside a ~$25M tender to give our early employees liquidity as we build for the long term. the round was led by Dream Ventures, a longtime supporter and one of our earliest investors, alongside Microsoft, Javelin, Flybridge, G Squared, Up Partners, and LG.

we’re also grateful to be backed by incredible industry leaders, including Guodong Zhang (co-founder of xAI), Andy Fang (CTO of DoorDash), Igor Babuschkin (co-founder of xAI), Behnam Neyshabur (founder of Mirendil), Jerry Tworek (ex-VP of Research at OpenAI), and many more.

data is on its way to becoming the largest industry humanity has ever seen, and we're certain this is just the beginning.

best,

text:
Over the last few months at @river_ai_inc we’ve developed what we believe is the best system in the world for building your own internal custom models, driven by 10 years of experience training top models at DeepMind, OpenAI and xAI.

In order to best support our customers, we’ve decided to do something radical: We also deploy our API on-prem on your compute cluster, and if you don’t have compute we will help you find it.

Again and again we’ve seen that custom models designed for your own internal workflows outperform top frontier models on performance, at a fraction of the cost (1 percent or less).

We’re just at the beginning of the custom model era, but its already clear that in the future more than 99% of LLM tokens will be generated on efficient custom models. The economics of it are just too powerful, and it’s far easier than people think once you have the right tools in place.

The reason why small models will dominate is due to the physics of deep learning: A general model that can do everything needs more capacity and training it on the whole distribution of all tasks is more challenging, so the model will be larger and more expensive, and wont perform perfectly on every task. A small model trained on a targeted domain usually outperforms it.
author: ycombinator
quoted_text:
We were able to fine tune an open weight model (Qwen3.5-9B) on proprietary internal data at @coinbase, and it out performed frontier models, at much lower cost and speed, for a specialized task (fraud prevention in this case).

I think we'll see more of this pattern inside companies. The frontier models are amazing generalists. But increasingly you'll see specialist models out perform on more narrow tasks, either working on teams, or by themselves.

We're making it easy to fine tune models internally for our employees. We even have a skill for it in our internal harness that makes it easy to spin these up and start training them:

"/fine-tune-and-serve-llm I want to fine-tune Qwen for payments risk review. help me get started"

I imagine we'll have some backend services that could be replaced entirely by this new architecture.

text:
When China figures out how to manufacture a product, their ability to scale is often greater than the rest of the world combined. We saw this with lithium batteries and solar, for example. 

SpaceX is a rare counter-example, where its mass to orbit is roughly an order of magnitude greater than the rest of the world, BUT China now does a majority of non-SpaceX mass to orbit. SpaceX is an anomaly in the matrix. 

Maybe RAM will be different, but RAM was a low margin commodity only ~3 years ago. LP5 and LP6 are designed to a common standard that China seems to be solving fast. 

Newer HBM architectures and things like an SRAM layer below logic and 3D stacking RAM on top of logic while finding a way to keep the logic cooled will be harder to solve.

text: Stay SAFU everyone
author: goyabean_eth
quoted_text:
Supply-chain attacks against hardware wallets aren't going away.

And that's something the entire crypto industry needs to take seriously.

Following the recent Ledger Nano X hardware implant research brought to public attention by @MagicalTux, I decided to investigate the attack myself.

Using an ESP32-S3, some basic electronics, and open-source tools, I was able to reproduce the display-bus interception concept and mirror my own Ledger Nano X screen onto another display.

The video shows my experimental reproduction.

What concerns me isn't just that information displayed by a hardware wallet can potentially be observed by an unauthorized hardware implant. It's how accessible the underlying techniques have become.

And this raises an even more interesting research question:

What if an implant didn't need to transmit stolen information at all?

Could a more sophisticated implant interfere with physical button inputs, manipulate user interactions, or exploit weaknesses in seed-generation workflows?

Could an attacker somehow cause a device to adopt a predictable recovery phrase without any external communication?

These are research hypotheses, NOT demonstrated attacks. Importantly, controlling the display or buttons alone does not mean an attacker can override the Secure Element's cryptographic randomness.

But they're questions worth investigating.

The lesson isn't that hardware wallets are useless, or that their manufacturers are malicious. Quite the opposite: many people in this industry have dedicated years to protecting users.

The problem is that security doesn't end at the Secure Element.

Manufacturing, distribution, logistics, hardware interfaces, firmware, physical access, and user verification all matter.

This is one of the reasons I'm building LeekWallet, an open-source, DIY hardware wallet designed around transparency, independent verification, accessible components, and user-controlled assembly.

I encourage everyone to do their own research, learn how their devices work, experiment responsibly, and consider building their own hardware wallets.

And please support open-source security projects. Independent research needs more than attention; it needs sustainable funding.

Special thanks to @MagicalTux for bringing this attack into the spotlight, and to @ETHGlobal and @thedaofund Security Fund for contributing to an ecosystem where independent builders and security researchers can thrive.

I'd also love to see more discussion around these issues from @ethereumfdn and @VitalikButerin.

If you believe open-source hardware security research matters, consider supporting LeekWallet through TheDAO Security Fund:

https://t.co/GmEQDPxmPE

https://t.co/uTjzKXlGzA

https://t.co/rZ5ubprNjy

Don't trust. Verify. And whenever possible, build.

#LeekWallet #OpenSource #HardwareWallet #Ethereum #SecurityResearch

I'd also like to acknowledge @Ledger and @DonjonLedger. Protecting users against sophisticated hardware attacks is an incredibly difficult challenge, and the work security teams do deserves recognition.

This research isn't about blaming manufacturers or undermining trust in hardware wallets. It's about understanding where trust boundaries can fail, encouraging independent verification, and strengthening the entire ecosystem.

Security research should bring builders, manufacturers, and independent researchers together, not divide them.

Responsible disclosure, open research, and collaboration make everyone safer.

text:
🐐It all starts with our fresh goat milk that I culture for 36 hours and turn into the creamiest, probiotic-rich, yogurt.

🫒From there, raw shea butter, olive oil, grass-fed tallow, coconut oil, and essential oils are blended together. 

🫗A cooled lye solution is then slowly blended with all the above ingredients, my soaps never reach above 90° F, this is to ensure  that all the ingredients stay viable.

✔️Lye is a reactant, after its done its job of saponification (turning fat/oil into soap)  none remains in the final product. I ensure this through "super fatting" the soap batter, which means adding an additional 5% butters and oils.

📝 True bar soap cannot be made without lye (sodium hydroxide) 
Even liquid castile soap is made with lye (potassium hydroxid) and its a great mild soap! ❤️

🫗The soap batter is poured into molds, kept cool, and they harden overnight.  

🧼They are then removed from the molds and placed on the shelf to cure and dry for 6-8 weeks. The longer they set, the milder they become.

text:
Generative Agents and LangChain rank recency by decay since the last access. So a one-off you mentioned ten minutes ago stays ahead of a habit you bring up every few days, until one of them gets used again.

ACT-R, a model of human memory from cognitive science, scores it differently. Every past use leaves its own trace that fades as a power law, and activation is the log of their sum. With its default decay (d = 0.5), the habit passes the one-off after about 2.7 hours. With decay values fitted to Twitter data, it takes 2 to 3.7 days. The equation is based on Anderson and Schooler (1991), who found that the odds of something coming back in news headlines, speech to children and email fall as a power function of the time since it last appeared.

The surprise was how little the curve itself mattered. In one hashtag study, plain most-recent came within a few percent of ACT-R, and as a cache the 1991 model barely beat random. The bigger gains came from other inputs, like how related a memory is to what's happening right now.

Everyone spent this year arguing about whether AI was a bubble. While they argued, it became the economy.

Per @a16z's new report, the AI infrastructure buildout accounts for nearly all net new construction spending, blue collar job growth, durable goods imports and IG issuance.

By a16z’s read, it’s the only thing pushing the economy forward right now.

@amazon, @Google, @Meta, @Microsoft and @Oracle spent $97B building this out in 2020 and roughly $777B this year, with over $1T forecast annually from 2027.

As a share of GDP, this buildout is now closing in on the US railroad boom.

But the cash has run out. Those five, plus @nvidia, borrowed near $50B a year for a decade, then $215B in 2025 and $320B in 2026.

Last week, @SpaceX opened talks for $40B more to buy Nvidia chips, four months after an $86B IPO and on top of a $25B bond.

Only the AI chips arrive on time. The transformers that feed them take 2 to 5 years. The turbines take 5 to 9. Order one today and it ships around 2031, behind a queue of 116 gigawatts.

As launch costs fell from roughly $9,000 a kilo to $3,568, annual tonnage to orbit climbed from 347 to over 3,000. Nearly 90% of everything launched this decade is commercial.

Orbit is the only place left with unlimited power and free cooling. Can you imagine what unlocks when over $1T a year of capex has nowhere else to go?

author: tushar_jain
quoted_text:
Walmart is selling real diamond earrings for $12.

Not a typo. Half-carat lab-grown diamonds, same carbon, graded by the same labs that grade the stone in your engagement ring. A jeweler can't tell them apart without a machine.

And that $12 price tag is why the company that invented the engagement ring is about to get sold for scrap.

De Beers ran the diamond trade for over a century. At its peak it controlled up to 90% of the world's rough supply, and when demand dipped it just locked diamonds in London vaults until prices came back. The slogan "A Diamond Is Forever" came from their ad agency in 1947. So did the rule that a ring should cost two months of your salary. Before that campaign, most American brides never got a diamond at all.

The whole thing held for 80 years because there were only so many mines. Then China started growing diamonds in reactors, and there's no vault on earth big enough to hide a factory's output.

Lab-grown wholesale prices have crashed roughly 96% from their peak, down to around $100 a carat. The Knot says 61% of engagement rings sold in 2025 had lab-grown center stones, up 239% since 2020. Even De Beers' own average selling price fell 32% in a year, to $105 a carat.

So Anglo American, which owns De Beers, has written it down by $6.8 billion in two years and is now in talks to sell the whole thing for about $1 billion. This is a company that was valued over $18 billion in 2001 and $13 billion as recently as 2011.

The stones coming out of the ground are the same as ever. The only scarce thing De Beers ever owned was the marketing, and marketing doesn't survive a $12 price tag at Walmart.

text:
my  #neatHack submission 

Introducing Headwind, an AI agent that runs a recruitment agency’s weekly review of the placement fees it’s counting on

A placement agency can have candidates at final interview, offers going out and fees expected next month. Those fees help the owner plan recruiter pay and other expenses.

Then a client pauses a role, fills it another way or stops replying. The forecast can keep counting on income whose timing has already changed

Headwind checks those assumptions

The owner uploads their clients, open roles, candidate stages, expected fees and cash figures. Headwind checks the agency’s records against company hiring data from Crustdata and saves the evidence with its source and date

A company hiring less doesn’t settle what happened to your particular role. A missing job ad doesn’t settle it either

Headwind separates supported changes from unanswered questions. An accepted offer keeps its expected fee assumption. A confirmed pause changes the receipt timing. An unresolved role gets a specific question for the account manager and stays visible in the Downside forecast

When the client’s reply is added, it reassesses that role, keeps the earlier decision in its history and updates the financial scenarios. Each update is read back from cfo_ai before it’s marked verified

In the labelled sample walkthrough, a simulated pause reduces November’s expected closing cash from $22,000 to $17,000. Another $4,000 remains unresolved, bringing Downside cash to $13,000

Each integration has a specific job:

• Crustdata supplies real company hiring data
• @neatlogs traces the runs, failures and before/after tests
• @EntireHQ captures the coding context behind our fix
• cfo_ai handles the forecast scenarios and Headwind’s own business plan, with @arithecfo 

The worker runs on AWS EC2 with saved progress in SQLite

We tested a worker crash followed by a lost response after cfo_ai had already saved an update. It recovered with 0 duplicate writes and 0 duplicate decisions in that test

it currently uses sample agency records and simulated replies, backed by real provider calls

Try the sample: https://t.co/YLupGoS2UW
Code, tests and evidence: https://t.co/3MdOw94PwW

text:
what a ledger spy implant looks like, and how to tell if yours is safe

this isn’t one shop in asia anymore. today a compromised nano x turned up in europe. its owner bought it in a mediamarkt store, europe’s biggest electronics chain. and the first ledger stax with an implant showed up too

the implant is a tiny extra board hidden inside a real ledger. it doesn’t hack the secure chip. it just reads the screen

when you set up your wallet, your 24 words show up on the display. the implant reads them and sends them out over its own SIM card. the ledger keeps working normally

that’s why the genuine check doesn’t catch it. the check only verifies the ledger chip, and the chip is real. the implant just taps the wire that carries pixels to the screen (pic 1, the yellow line)

the early implants are easy to spot: loose wires, an extra board, a small no-name battery. that’s the mediamarkt device in pic 3

the newest ones look normal. original battery, the implant painted black under the screen, chip markings scraped off. the only giveaways: a thin black wire along the top edge (pic 2) and the foam pad behind the screen missing

the stax has the same thing inside: a cellular modem a real stax has no reason to carry (pic 4)

and it’s a product line. the antennas carry part numbers: “AC-A2016-NANO-V1.1”, “AC-A2205-NANO-X” with a “eurasian version” label, “AC-A2014-STAX-V1.1”. one per ledger model, plus regional versions. someone has been making these for about a year

they’ve turned up in japan, in southeast asia with the drained cryptobilis buyers, in a mediamarkt in europe, and in the stax posted by an account based in malaysia. the mediamarkt one was bought on aug 26 and never drained, according to its owner. he thinks it was a returned device put back on the shelf. they can sit on your words for months

to check yours, open it with ledger’s official guide. you want the original battery on the board, clean battery pads, nothing orange, no extra black board, no wire on the top edge, the foam pad in place

found something, or bought from anyone other than @Ledger ? don’t set it up. if you already did, treat your 24 words as leaked, even if it never touched the internet. buy a new device straight from ledger, make a new seed, move everything

in its latest update ledger says every confirmed case so far is a cryptobilis device, and calls the number “limited”. not a word yet about the europe device or the stax

don’t wait for an official announcement. protect yourself now
author: crypto_bitlord7
quoted_text:
so about the $86m ledger drain. everyone’s screaming “ledger got hacked” again. i spent the evening digging and it’s dumber and scarier than that

there’s a shop in malaysia called cryptobilis that sells hardware wallets. ledger has it listed as an official authorized reseller since at least 2022, for malaysia, indonesia and the philippines. legit shop, real devices, years of normal customers

this spring the founders sell it. the deal comes with an NDA: they can’t tell anyone about the sale until october 19

by august the company registry shows one owner with 100%. some guy from heilongjiang, china

the shop keeps running like nothing happened. the site, the name and the “authorized by ledger” badge all stay up

then on oct 8 @MagicalTux posts photos of a ledger he cracked open. hidden under the screen there’s an extra little board with an LTE modem and an eSIM. it just watches the display. you set up your wallet, your 24 words show up, and they get sent out over mobile data. ledger’s genuine check doesn’t catch it because the actual ledger chip is real. his device came from malaysia

https://t.co/vRuBM0xIfR

that post does 120k views

22 hours later someone sweeps everything. 203 BTC hits two addresses in literally one block. ~$58m USDT moves on tron in the same hour. i added up all the wallets: ~$91m

about 7 hours after that ledger says “we’re investigating” and asks cryptobilis to pause sales

cryptobilis is still on ledger’s site as an authorized reseller

to be fair, nobody has officially tied the new owner to the bugged devices yet, and ledger hasn’t confirmed how it happened. but read it as a business plan:

get authorized, sell real stuff for years, quietly sell the company under an NDA, keep the badge, ship devices that phone home, then drain everything the second someone notices

and was ledger even told the shop got sold? nobody’s said so

“authorized reseller” means ledger trusted whoever ran the shop back in 2022. says nothing about who runs it today

bought your hardware wallet anywhere but the manufacturer? open it up today, ledger literally has a guide for that. then move to a fresh seed on a device bought direct

wonder who’s going to answer for this: the chinese frontman from heilongjiang, the shop’s previous owners, or ledger itself

@Ledger clearly needs to keep a much closer eye on who they call official resellers, and take way more responsibility for who sells their devices and how

text:
This selloff in memory stocks makes absolutely NO sense to me.

$MU, $SNDK, Samsung and SK Hynix are getting hit after China's CXMT announced progress on its new 4F² DRAM architecture, with plans to introduce DDR5 server memory using the technology by the end of 2026. For those unfamiliar, this technology is designed to pack more memory cells into the same amount of space, potentially improving chip density and manufacturing efficiency.

Now, I want to make something clear. CXMT is absolutely becoming a legitimate competitor because acording to TrendForce, CXMT has already captured roughly 9.5% of global DRAM revenue, up from 7.6% the previous quarter, making it the fourth largest DRAM manufacturer globally. The company is also expanding aggressively, with new manufacturing facilities in Shanghai and Hefei targeting more than 600,000 wafers per month, potentially doubling its manufacturing capacity. On top of that, CXMT has reportedly started mass production of its G5 DRAM platform and LPDDR6 memory, while its new 4F² architecture could make memory production even more efficient.

But here's why I think the market is getting WAY ahead of itself. First, announcing a new memory architecture and successfully manufacturing it at scale are two completely different things. CXMT still needs to prove it can deliver competitive yields, pricing, reliability, and production volumes. Second, we're currently dealing with an enormous memory supply shortage, particularly as hyperscalers continue increasing AI infrastructure spending. Even if CXMT successfully doubles its capacity, that doesn't automatically mean the industry becomes oversupplied. Demand for memory is expected to grow substantially over the next several years, and we're already seeing manufacturers secure longer term supply agreements with customers.

Third, this announcement is primarily focused on conventional DDR5 server memory, NOT HBM. That's an important distinction because HBM is becoming one of the most valuable parts of the memory industry, with Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix benefiting from enormous AI demand. And SanDisk primarily manufactures NAND flash memory, not DRAM. So selling $SNDK specifically because of a DDR5 technology announcement seems even more questionable. Now, that doesn't mean CXMT won't eventually put pressure on conventional DRAM prices. Increased Chinese manufacturing capacity is absolutely something investors should monitor, especially over the longer term but I think investors are confusing a legitimate long term competitive threat with an immediate change in industry fundamentals. Nothing about today's announcement suddenly creates millions of additional memory chips, eliminates existing supply shortages, or changes the amount of memory needed to power AI infrastructure. I've been saying this for months. The amount of memory we're going to need over the next decade is INSANE.  Bullish on memory, if you want to see how I’m investing around the companies that could benefit from this massive increase in global memory demand, check out my portfolio below.

text:
Model Benchmarks Are Worthless 

How can a model score 24% and 59% on the same 113 coding tasks?

It happens when you vary the harness that wraps it. 

I’ve increasingly ignored most of the recent model leaderboard results. Partly from exhaustion and partly because improvements in a ranking don’t show up in the actual work. 

So I asked the 8090 Labs team to measure what the leaderboards skip: the model and the harness together, on real bug fixes and features from open-source projects.

8090 Labs ran 7 models through 5 harnesses. 

Here are a few results I didn't expect:

- Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 scored 41% in Claude Code and 61% in OpenAI's Codex. It made 28 tool calls at the median in one and 66 in the other.

- The cheapest runs weren't the cheapest work. GLM in Codex cost $0.22 a run and $0.93 per success. In Pi it cost $0.25 a run and $0.43 per success.

- GLM passed a task on both attempts 51 times in one harness and 16 times in another.

- GPT-5.6 Sol and Grok 4.6 barely cared which harness they were in.

The bottom line is that if you're picking a model/harness combo off a model-only leaderboard, you're making a critical decision based on only half the information.

"Built in the Storm" - $OPEN 

Sometimes there just isn’t a clean answer to the “why.”

The fundamentals can still be there.
The foundation can still be getting built.
And the stock can still sit at 52-week lows.

That’s max pain.

This is where conviction gets tested the most, because nothing you say, post, buy, or sell changes the tape in that moment.

You start asking yourself:

Do I sell?
Do I buy the dip?
Do I change the thesis?

Sometimes the best decision is no decision at all.

Let the storm pass.
Let management keep building.
Let the thesis prove itself.

For me, this feels like one of those times.

Stay grounded in the work you’ve already done.
Separate the stock price from the business.
Watch the execution, the numbers, and whether the thesis is still intact.

If the thesis breaks, react to that.
If the thesis is still strengthening while the price is weakening, then patience may be the hardest trade of all.

Markets can stay painful longer than we want.

But eventually, fundamentals and execution get their chance to speak.

After my last post, lot of common investors like me questioned that how can you say stock market can do well, despite rising dollar & bond yield and that too when markets has been consistently falling since last 2 years....

So, today I am going to share my portfolio performance to educate retail investors that Individual stocks and portfolios can perform very differently from any index.

Here’s my portfolio performance since 3 July 2023:

📈 My portfolio: +184.27% 📊 Nifty 50: +16.57% 📊 Nifty Smallcap 250: +65.18%

The real lesson? 👇

An index is not the entire stock market.
Nifty 50 represents large-cap companies. Nifty Smallcap 250 represents small-cap companies.
Individual stocks and portfolios can perform very differently from either index.

Why can a portfolio outperform?

Potential reasons include:

• Stock selection
• Sector allocation
• Earnings growth
• Buying at attractive valuations
• Portfolio concentration and risk-taking

What about a rising dollar, bond yields, or a falling Nifty?

These factors can create headwinds, but they don't affect every company equally.
A strong business with improving earnings can outperform even when the broader market struggles.

Macro matters. But business fundamentals and valuation matter too.

Key takeaway for retail investors:

Don't confuse index performance with the performance of every stock.

Study businesses, earnings, valuations, and risk.

Invest with knowledge, not assumption

Please follow my page for more practical insights on investing and business fundamentals. Share this thread with someone who wants to learn.

UPDATE: I can confirm that the Ledger supply chain is compromised in Europe as well. @Ledger should initiate an immediate product recall to protect users.

I just purchased a second device from a different Mediamarkt location today, recorded the unboxing process, and discovered spyware once again (video linked in the second tweet).

The device was compromised in the exact same manner, featuring identical modifications (such as additional cables and an LTE module). This indicates its a widespread issue rather than an isolated incident, potentially affecting Ledger inventory across MediaMarkt and Saturn stores throughout Europe (comprising over 1,000 stores across 11 countries).

My initial hypothesis was that these devices were returns that looked unopened to the employees and were just sold again as new however, a MediaMarkt employee confirmed that the device I purchased was not a return, and that returned Ledgers are sent directly back to the manufacturer rather than resold.

Store records show the inventory originated from Aqipa GmbH. While Ledger's CTO was unsure if Aqipa serves as the direct distributor between Ledger and MediaMarkt, it appears to be the case. Given that Aqipa distributes across Europe, any physical retail store receiving stock through them may be at risk.

I sent the first ledger to mark and the second one is going to ledger now, so that they can analyse it.
If you purchased a ledger from anyone other than the official ledger store, make sure to check your device!!

text:
Pacing is out the window. For it to work, every American lab needed to be on board, Mark Zuckerberg has repeatedly made it clear that he is not interested. One defection among US labs breaks it all, as the others will be forced to accelerate or get passed. Mark has a staggering amount of compute and has been all in on compute capex for years; even in the face of some investor opposition he never stopped building his infra once. He said on the the earnings call a couple of years ago that he'd rather overspend now, and potentially even be wrong, than not have the compute when he needed it for the next 10x. He's finally hitting his stride, and he is not going to slow down.

For Team Pacing to solve a defection like this, they would have needed a supportive, pro-Pacing administration that was passing capability regulations and was willing to use the power of the federal government to enforce them and bring noncompliant labs into line. They don't have any of this. In fact, it's the opposite! Mark has Trump's ear, and President Trump, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jensen are completely aligned on policy; It's full speed ahead, and if you want to pace yourself, go ahead, but don't tell anyone else what to do. This breaks Pacing.

None of this changes until 2029 at the earliest, and to me, 2029 is past the ASI window. The last election, as it turns out, really was the most important one in history.

text:
What is $PAPER worth to the market right now? Looking at @paperstrategy_ can help.

Its current snapshot (balance sheet) is $2.47M market cap against $737k in remaining capital + $219k in rewards + 94.2M PAPER.

So, ($2.47M − $737k − $219k) / 94.2M = ~$0.016 per PAPER.

Attributing the $1.51M mcap entirely to its PAPER holdings gives us an implied price. Those tokens’ future earnings are already priced in.

ofc this ignores that PSTR also has a business: trading taxes fund further accumulation, and strategy + execution risk. The market can attach a premium or discount to all of that.

1.6 cents per PAPER is what the market is signalling now. Right now it costs about 3.4 cents to mint paper, less if you hedge.

author: iruletrenches
quoted_text:
前段时间，我说过看到了科学家在研究：真实物理硬件的 source of truth。今天学者 Joooooo 把他的研究：Bard（吟游诗人）公开了，包括其完整技术文章、注释、GitHub 代码以及最新 v8g 芯片版图。

我认为，很多人可能低估了这项研究对 TapeOut Protocol 的意义。

这件事最重要的突破，是它开始展示一种全新的可能性：让 AI 的计算逻辑成为可以永久追溯、公开验证、跨越不同物理载体重新执行的数字资产。

Bard 本身并不是大型语言模型。它只有约 97 万个三值权重，是一个基于 TinyStories 的五层 Transformer，词表仅 192 个 Token。

但作者使用公开的 SKY130 工艺和开源 EDA 工具，将完整模型转化为数字逻辑，再完成一张面积仅 15.09 mm² 的芯片版图。

我核对了 GitHub 发布资料：

• 60 个 Mask ROM 存储模型权重
• 权重宏面积由 7.44 mm² 缩小至 1.10 mm²
• DRC 零违例，LVS 匹配，天线问题完成修复
• 三个功能测试用例与参考程序的 Token 及执行周期一致
• 完整 OASIS 版图约 11.16 MB，作者称已存入链上

这里必须说明，Bard 尚未实际流片，仍有部分电气约束需要处理。

但是，我认为它已经展示出一条值得研究的技术路线。

AI Model → Deterministic Circuit → On-chain Execution / Physical Silicon

其中有三个特别重要的方向。

1️⃣ Full On-chain-state Circuit（全链态电路）

作者提出，芯片只是电路的一次物理实例化。

真正能够被长期继承的，是完整的数字蓝图。

同一套计算逻辑，既可以在 TapeOut 的 NAND/LATCH 环境中执行，也能够映射为真实半导体设计。

两者内部实现不一定相同，但可以依据确定性的计算规则进行验证。

当前 Bard 的完整网表还没有全部部署上链，但这一方向已经有较小规模的链上电路实验作为基础。

2️⃣ AI-assisted Silicon Design

Bard 的另一项价值，是作者通过 Claude 及两个 AI Agents 协作完成大量设计、验证和物理实现工作。

结合开源 PDK、开源 EDA 和可验证电路，芯片设计可能逐步从高度专业化的产业流程，走向更多个人开发者和开源社区。

这也许比单独制造一颗 AI 芯片更有长期影响力。

3️⃣ Open Silicon Infrastructure

如果未来能够把模型权重、逻辑网表、验证报告、GDS/OASIS 版图及链上身份统一成开放标准，TapeOut 就有机会发展出一种新的基础设施：

让硬件逻辑像开源软件一样能够被分享、验证、复现和持续演化。

当然，目前还不能把文件哈希一致直接等同于实体芯片可信。真实硅片制造、测试和身份认证，仍然是重要的未完成环节。

我认为 Bard 最值得期待的是完成第一次实际流片，以及将完整电路部署到 TapeOut 网络。

这将帮助我们验证一个真正重要的问题：

一段计算逻辑，是否能够同时拥有链上的数字生命与现实世界的物理载体？

过去，Crypto 让数字资产拥有了可验证的所有权。

未来，TapeOut 可能进一步探索让计算逻辑本身拥有可验证、可复现、可组合的存在形式。

Bard 还远不是这个愿景的终点。

但它可能正在推开其中一扇门。

Github：https://t.co/TxyJOy6M6q

#TapeOut Builder Culture 🦾 @TapeOutWorld

quoted_text:
最近把 $virtual 、 solana:7VertkgF9KLhxxJXHX6uaWuoYZTP9LdGj2bWmVXVpump 、 robinhood:0x18e674231a58c239dc7daedcffe15ec3a24cff5c 、 $Claus 和  ethereum:0x7987f03462200b3d8a072e02c89a8a41dcb124ee  放在一起看，感觉这条叙事开始有意思了：AI 不光能发帖、管钱包，还能参与一个币的交易规则。🤔

这几个项目，做的其实是不同层面的事。

Virtuals 偏向把 AI agent 做成币，强制配对， solana:7VertkgF9KLhxxJXHX6uaWuoYZTP9LdGj2bWmVXVpump  更进一步，给每个币配一个脑子和金库，用交易手续费养它，让它发内容、空投、回购。但池子怎么交易，还是按 Pump 的规则来。

robinhood:0x18e674231a58c239dc7daedcffe15ec3a24cff5c  做的是交易规则：发币时选好功能，积木搭建，上线后焊死，创建者和平台都不能随便改。

⭐️ $Claus  最有意思的地方，是币不用重发，池子不用重建，后面的规则还能继续变。

比如根据天气调整手续费里多少拿去回购、多少拿去加池。名字也能改，持有人手里的币还是原来那个地址。以前想加新玩法，往往得发个新币；现在可以在原来的币上继续做。

不过得分清楚：能改规则，不代表 AI 已经可以随心所欲地创造金融产品。目前改规则的钥匙还在项目钱包手里，借贷、杠杆这些也还是后续方向。
👉这个权限让它有想象力，也意味着你得信任掌握钥匙的人。

再看 ethereum:0x7987f03462200b3d8a072e02c89a8a41dcb124ee ，逻辑就从“哪个实验会火”，变成了“这些实验从谁的工厂里出来”。

这里说的是 Programmable 的平台币  ethereum:0x7987f03462200b3d8a072e02c89a8a41dcb124ee， $Claus  就是通过 Programmable 的以太坊发射路由部署的。

Claus 自己收的那笔约 2% 项目费，拿去养 Claus；V4 吃的是另外一层平台过路费。费用在 ETH 收，V4 在 Robinhood 链上，实际有没有买回来、烧掉多少，还得看执行记录。

所以我看这两个的兴趣点很明确：

$Claus  值得看，是因为它把“一个币上线之后还能怎么进化”做成了具体实验。
0x1b54E762aa34CF6E28E9C082F2848e28E45DA6b8

ethereum:0x7987f03462200b3d8a072e02c89a8a41dcb124ee  值得看，是因为如果这类实验越来越多，它有机会持续收过路费，且做一个高质量 HookV4+AI 发射工厂。

author: FigoETH
quoted_text:
UPDATE: I can confirm that the Ledger supply chain is compromised in Europe as well. @Ledger should initiate an immediate product recall to protect users.

I just purchased a second device from a different Mediamarkt location today, recorded the unboxing process, and discovered spyware once again (video linked in the second tweet).

The device was compromised in the exact same manner, featuring identical modifications (such as additional cables and an LTE module). This indicates its a widespread issue rather than an isolated incident, potentially affecting Ledger inventory across MediaMarkt and Saturn stores throughout Europe (comprising over 1,000 stores across 11 countries).

My initial hypothesis was that these devices were returns that looked unopened to the employees and were just sold again as new however, a MediaMarkt employee confirmed that the device I purchased was not a return, and that returned Ledgers are sent directly back to the manufacturer rather than resold.

Store records show the inventory originated from Aqipa GmbH. While Ledger's CTO was unsure if Aqipa serves as the direct distributor between Ledger and MediaMarkt, it appears to be the case. Given that Aqipa distributes across Europe, any physical retail store receiving stock through them may be at risk.

I sent the first ledger to mark and the second one is going to ledger now, so that they can analyse it.
If you purchased a ledger from anyone other than the official ledger store, make sure to check your device!!

I used Claude Opus 5.5 to design a little blueberry home for one of our Mac minis.

The phone is its face, so the enclosure needed a built-in stand. Getting there meant moving the phone so it didn’t block the Mac’s ports, changing the backrest to clear the camera bump, and figuring out how to print it with the filament I actually had.

I only had one 250g spool of blue left so I split the design into blue parts and separate green leaves and trim (leaf skirt), then I printed and assembled them on our Bambu H2S.

The tiny leaves went in with tweezers. They’re such a small detail, but they make the whole thing and it's so cute.

author: iruletrenches
quoted_text:
🚀 PROM ecosystem × @TapeOutWorld × @MovaChain 🤝

You can verify a contract. You cannot verify the app in front of you: its frontend, its entry point, and its version sit on ordinary servers, DNS, and gateways, and nothing on-chain says whether what loaded is the real thing.

TapeOut is working to make the application itself an on-chain object: entry points, versions, service declarations, and content hashes written as records anyone can read and check. Mova brings the settlement rail, with stablecoins such as USD1 from @worldlibertyfi as the unit those services are priced in.

At PROM, we're building the middle layer —the condition. A gateway served the request, a frontend was delivered, a version checked out, and that fact, rather than an invoice, is what releases the payment.

More updates soon. 🚀

text:
Last week, Robinhood Chain turned 100 days old.

In the history of TradFi, which took generations to change, that’s a blink of an eye. Onchain, where markets move from idea to existence overnight and assets reach people in milliseconds, a lot can happen — and a lot has.

Robinhood Chain was built to close that gap.

100 days is early days in the life of a new chain, but our initial growth says a lot about why we built it.

✔️ 190+ Stock Tokens are live, and they reached 200K holders faster than on any chain yet. That’s people in 120+ countries gaining exposure to U.S. equities, access that’s still out of reach for billions of people around the world.

✔️ $15B in Stock Token DEX volume proves what’s possible once utility is brought onchain and made composable: new liquidity, new features, and, on Robinhood Chain, pairings people never imagined. 

Giving builders the tools to experiment, form new communities, and ship globally is why building onchain is so powerful and unique. 100 days of Stock Tokens in DeFi has made that clear. From perps to agents and lending markets, the opportunities are out there for anyone who wants to build.

✔️ $1B+ deposited on Morpho on Robinhood Chain. Lending and borrowing, open to anyone, in a world where 1.3 billion adults still don’t have a bank account.

✔️ Robinhood Chain has been the #1 L2 for daily active traders since launch, with $1B+ in TVL and $99B+ in cumulative DEX volume. None of this would be possible without everyone who came here to build and every trader who jumped into the trenches from day one.

Rome wasn’t built in a day (or 100 days), and Robinhood Chain won’t be either. We have more work to do, and we’re excited about what’s next. 

More users, more experiments, more milestones, and more reasons why TradFi and DeFi building on the same rails unlocks a better, more open future for finance.

The next 100 days starts now.

I, along with the rest of the Deno company, am joining Cloudflare!

I'm motivated by abstractions that give leverage at scale. The Cloudflare workers programming model is a hermetic computing abstraction that truly embodies the old Sun Microsystems tagline "The Network Is the Computer". The programming abstractions that Kenton designed really force scalability. If you squint your eyes you might even conceive of it as a distributed high-level operating system.

The only major problem with this distributed operating system is that practically people only use it inside of Cloudflare. Cloudflare is an amazing service for nearly all applications - but there are many situations when you might need it to run elsewhere.

I want to solve this problem and make the Workers programming model the default way you write server-side application code. 

The time is ripe for new abstractions too - what software we run and how we run it are changing quickly with AI. The number of agents is exploding and I don't think they all need a Linux VM. A much more lightweight Durable Object would suffice for many applications. I'm super keen to talk to people who want to self-host agents at scale on DOs - msg me!

text: SSMs had the nice asymptotics but kept missing out on the inference goodies Transformers get for free like spec decode and quantization. Turns out we were just not caching the right thing. Same IO-aware trick behind FlashAttention, Mamba scan, paged KV. A lot of the big wins weren’t new architectures, just people taking memory IO seriously.
author: teortaxesTex
quoted_text:
ReplaySSM now runs in production in GLM-5.3-Flash and Kimi-K3, and ships in TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, FlashInfer, and SGLang!

It speeds up standard decoding (up to 1.47x) and speculative decoding (up to 2.1x), and now also enables a low-precision SSM state whose rounding error never propagates through the recurrence.

Building on our earlier ReplaySSM work, we collaborated with @NVIDIA to pin down what the method really unlocks. Caching SSM inputs instead of the state is what ReplaySSM does. What it changes is that computing the output and updating the state can be separated during decoding. All three gains follow from that separation.

Joint blog post, paper, and code with @NVIDIA and @tri_dao 👇

A lot of today's chip design workflows, tools, and abstractions were built around the limitations of humans and traditional algorithms.

quoted_text:
AI will make chip design faster. It won't make chips easier. I sat down with Raghu Raghuram and Guido Appenzeller at a16z to talk about what's really constraining the AI buildout. It's not just compute.

1) Silicon still takes quarters to manufacture, no matter how fast we design
2) Memory bandwidth and advanced packaging are huge choke points
3) Copper is giving way to optical
4) Energy capacity is becoming economic capacity

I also think today's explosion of specialized AI chips will consolidate around fewer architectures. And I'd love to see what a "VMware for agents" looks like when infrastructure is built for them instead of for us.

author: Shaughnessy119
quoted_text:
Renting vs Owning Your AI Intelligence

The American dream was owning a home. I think the future version is owning your AI brain. Something you build intelligence equity in instead of renting it and enriching the man

Over the next few decades everyone is going to accumulate a ton of intelligence around AI. Your memories, context, skills, workflows, integrations, databases, emails, corrections, operating knowledge and all the apps you build and everything in between including your psychology and your dreams. It will become one of the most valuable assets a person or a company owns

The scarce thing is no longer access to intelligence, it is the accumulated system around the model that makes intelligence yours.

The question becomes do you rent that intelligence or own it?

Path one is the default. You spend your life, personal or business, working inside ChatGPT or Claude. And to be fair, you can genuinely build really cool things this way. Memory, projects, custom GPTs, skills, connectors, automations and most people will probably go this route.

Everything you create runs inside their product. There is no runtime you can take with you, nothing you can fork, and no way to point what you built at a different provider's model. You inherit every product decision they make on pricing, features, memory behavior and what they allow you to do or not to do (censorship on security asks or medical or otherwise). 

You can export your content, but content is not the system. An export is not a runnable copy of your memory, tools, automations and routing. When you leave, the system stays behind.

Path two is you own the entire layer around the model. A whole ecosystem of open source agents is emerging to make this possible. The strongest release in my view is @NousResearch's Hermes Agent. Most alternatives are developer frameworks you have to assemble yourself. Hermes is a complete agent you just run. 

Here is what you own with it

- Host locally or on the cloud and you own everything
- Persistent memory, searchable session history, databases and every interaction from day one
- Editable personality, skills, workflows and scripts
- Subagents, tools and scheduled automations
- Model and provider choice and MCP connectors
- Portable profiles, histories and backups
- Switch models at will for cost, reasoning, or to avoid censorship and model restrictions
- MIT licensed runtime you can self host, fork and modify
- Every application, automated cron job or integration you have created in its entirety
- Transcend a single walled garden with access to any integration accessible via an API/MCP.
- Eventually you’ll click a button and fine tune an open source model based on all of your own accumulated data and you can use it to power your agent

ChatGPT and Claude have versions of half this list. Memory, skills, connectors, scheduled tasks. The difference is physical. Theirs are features inside their app, backed by their database, living on their servers. In Hermes every one of these is on a computer you control. Your memory is a database you can open. Your skills are text files you can read, edit and copy. Your automations are cron entries you can inspect. Your agent's personality is a config you can rewrite. Files can be backed up, moved, forked and pointed at any model on earth. Features can only be used. When you own you can tear down the walls and rebuild the kitchen.

For a person, this is the AI brain you build and control for life. It compounds everything you choose to preserve and moves with you across jobs, devices and providers. Swap models at will for cost or reasoning, or run several at once through Mixture of Agents.

You'll never log in one day to find your entire AI brain, everything you built around a model over decades, gone because of a ban, a deprecation or a policy change.

For a business, this is a core asset the company actually owns. Employee knowledge becomes company owned skills, workflows and automations that remain after people leave and grow enterprise wide while they are there. That system can be deployed across the org, licensed out, or transferred within the business. Sharing your Hermes build and skills to new employees and enterprise wide will be a whole new era of productivity.

Net, whatever you build with Hermes as a business you own entirely. You can license it out or sell the agent itself. The agent itself can become the product. You can't sell your ChatGPT or Claude session. You can obviously sell what you create with ChatGPT/Claude in chat but you can't sell the core AI architecture you've built around the model.

Here is the part I think people will only get in hindsight. Models are becoming cheaper, better and more interchangeable every year. GLM 5.2/Kimi are so good that the government is considering banning them because they are so cheap to use it threatens the U.S. funding capex cycle. The scarce thing is no longer access to intelligence, it is the accumulated system around the model that makes intelligence yours.

When you’re in virtual reality side by side with your agent exploring the virtual cosmos or its 2am and you’re discussing the next company idea, you’re going to want your AI to be the full encapsulation of everything you’ve built over the years. That juice, that style, that data accumulated around the model in your AI brain is where the crazy stuff will happen. Evolutionary jumps come from variation. A world where everyone runs the same three models is a monoculture of ideas. A hyper personalized architecture around the model (or unique fine tuned models themselves) is the variation, the EV+ differentiation that produces the outlier results, companies and agents. 

We’ve already seen Harnesses greatly upskill models. Now imagine how much a personalized harness upskills your entire AI experience when you build it over time.

Here is an example with zenith harness taking base models to the top of FrontierSWE via adaptive self improvement https://t.co/58gbcs70Dw

Let’s Walk Down A Decade in Each Path

Ten years in ChatGPT or Claude and it will genuinely know you. Your projects, your preferences, your whole history. But let's look at what actually compounded. Their system got smarter about you, and their system is identical for every user on earth using one company's models, their prices, their rules, their memory format, their ceiling. You cannot rewire how it remembers, restructure how it works, or point your decade of accumulated context at a better or cheaper model. Every correction you gave them deepened their retention moat and, depending on your settings, may have trained their next model.

Ten years with Hermes agent and that same decade compounded into a system you hold and have been innovating on the whole time. You rewired its memory, stacked hundreds of skills it wrote from watching you work, wired in your own subagents, tools, databases, automations and integrations, tuned its personality and its routing until it fits nobody on earth but you. Depending on the scaffolding around a model (the agent harness) your experience with AI takes a huge leap forward, as much as a full model generation upgrade. And that is from generic harnesses built for everyone. Now imagine the harness effect at the level of each person. This is an architecture engineered around your brain, your workflows and your taste for ten straight years. The model underneath is just a component. GLM today, Kimi tomorrow, local when it matters, eventually a model fine tuned on your own decade of data. With Hermes agent you are building the entire scaffolding and architecture around a model that grows and compounds over decades which provides a truly unique experience.

I strongly believe people will want to own their AI brain long term (and everything built around it) and Hermes agents will create, and in themselves become, massive companies and projects in their own right. The journey will start with manually building your agent, then granting it some automation, then fully graduating it to autonomy. 

Even Sam Altman from OpenAI agrees with the need for Open Source harnesses: https://t.co/4UL4rOeErn

You don't have to be a master AI builder with some grand plan, you just have to decide you want to own your AI brain you'll spend decades building. All the cool stuff will come later

Start your multi decade journey and own your AI brain for life: https://t.co/CUQAcvhJmu

Ty to Kevin Simback for thoughts and comments

author: 0xlorik
quoted_text:
Why Extended is pursuing a regulated path in Europe

TLDR: European retail already trades inside licensed apps, and regulated platforms typically need regulated venues they can integrate. Extended is building one. Builder codes let partners plug Extended into their own product: through the existing venue for self-custody users where available, and through the regulated venue for regulated clients once live.

Europe has close to 10,000 fintech companies, and hundreds of licensed investment firms and credit institutions. Most are exploring new ways to engage their retail user base, and perps are consistently near the top of the list. All of them are potential clients for a regulated exchange.

That market opportunity drove our decision to build a regulated venue in Europe:
1. Retail is the user base we are building the regulated offering for. We have said before that sustainable growth is built on product quality, distribution and community rather than financial incentives. For a trading product, the largest pool of users is retail, and reaching it is a distribution problem.
2. Perp DEXs processed roughly $600 billion in volume over the past 30 days. CFD brokers alone show the size of the addressable market: around $30 trillion a month, with a large share of it in Europe. The largest platforms already earn most of their volume outside FX, in equities, indices, commodities and crypto. On-chain perps is a market we know well and intend to keep serving, but the larger opportunity sits next to it: tens of millions of retail traders already active on regulated platforms, many of whom have no access to perps today.
3. There are three retail markets at the scale that matters: the US, Europe and Asia. The US is the most contested, with many major exchanges and brokers competing for the same users and a long licensing path. Asia has high perps penetration but regulatory approaches vary by jurisdiction. Europe is where we are starting, and we will look at other regulated markets as and when it makes sense.
4. Regulated crypto derivatives in Europe have only recently expanded. Kraken, Coinbase and Bitstamp (owned by Robinhood) launched futures for EU clients over the past 18 months, each using regulatory infrastructure obtained through an acquisition of a licensed investment firm or exchange. That route is open to a handful of firms with the balance sheet for it, but for the far larger group of fintechs and brokers with users and no perps infrastructure, it is not. Our model is to offer builder codes on both venues: a way for partners to plug perps into their own apps, route users’ orders to the venue and earn a share of the fees. Self-custody wallets can integrate with the existing venue where available. Regulated brokers and fintechs will be able to use the regulated venue once it is live.
5. A regulated perps setup takes significant time and resources to build from scratch, and many fintechs lack the product and market expertise to run it well, starting with established market-maker relationships. For smaller players the economics may not work. For larger ones, regulated builder codes cut time to market, especially inside slow-moving large organisations, and deliver a quality product from day one.
6. The demand is clear. We are already in conversations with wallets, CFD brokers and fintechs across Europe, and we repeatedly hear the same request: a regulated venue with a broad range of crypto and RWA markets they can integrate.

Importantly, this does not change our DeFi offering or our commitment to the early community. The existing venue stays for crypto-native users where it is available. The regulated venue adds a new distribution channel and a new user base. 

Europe is the first step. Over time, we expect to replicate the same model in other markets, including the US. Our plan is subject to the relevant regulatory authorisations, and we will share specifics as they are confirmed. At a high level, we have an initial route to market, followed by a transition to our own licences.

BREAKING: 🇫🇷 A major cyberattack has hit supermarket refrigeration systems across France, reportedly causing fresh and frozen food to spoil after hackers remotely manipulated temperature controls.

According to BFMTV, the attack began overnight from Sunday into Monday, targeting older versions of refrigeration-control software supplied by Danish company Danfoss.

The attackers allegedly exploited the systems’ defrosting function, forcing refrigeration equipment to heat continuously instead of keeping products cold. Temperatures were reportedly set as high as 50°C, destroying entire stocks of food within hours.

Several major supermarket chains have been affected, including Intermarché, Super U and https://t.co/7bHBi61WPZ. Metro stores and independent businesses, including butcher shops also have been impacted.

Around 150 Intermarché stores are reportedly affected, according to industry sources cited by BFMTV. The full number of affected locations remains unclear.

The financial damage is already significant. In Haguenau, Alsace, an Intermarché store reportedly lost its entire frozen-food stock, worth approximately €50,000. A nearby Super U allegedly had to discard both fresh and frozen products, with losses estimated at €220,000. An https://t.co/7bHBi61WPZ store in the same town was also affected, although its losses had not yet been calculated.

The combined losses reported at the Intermarché and Super U stores in Haguenau alone amount to around €270,000. Nationwide damage could reach several million euros.

Intermarché reportedly confirmed the incident in an internal communication, warning that several stores had suffered losses of frozen products. Coopérative U also acknowledged the attack and established crisis teams to assist affected stores and coordinate with refrigeration specialists.

Technical investigations are ongoing, and the full extent of the damage has yet to be established.

Authorities and companies are still working to determine the full circumstances of the attack. The identity of the perpetrators has not been confirmed.

text:
Why Extended is pursuing a regulated path in Europe

TLDR: European retail already trades inside licensed apps, and regulated platforms typically need regulated venues they can integrate. Extended is building one. Builder codes let partners plug Extended into their own product: through the existing venue for self-custody users where available, and through the regulated venue for regulated clients once live.

Europe has close to 10,000 fintech companies, and hundreds of licensed investment firms and credit institutions. Most are exploring new ways to engage their retail user base, and perps are consistently near the top of the list. All of them are potential clients for a regulated exchange.

That market opportunity drove our decision to build a regulated venue in Europe:
1. Retail is the user base we are building the regulated offering for. We have said before that sustainable growth is built on product quality, distribution and community rather than financial incentives. For a trading product, the largest pool of users is retail, and reaching it is a distribution problem.
2. Perp DEXs processed roughly $600 billion in volume over the past 30 days. CFD brokers alone show the size of the addressable market: around $30 trillion a month, with a large share of it in Europe. The largest platforms already earn most of their volume outside FX, in equities, indices, commodities and crypto. On-chain perps is a market we know well and intend to keep serving, but the larger opportunity sits next to it: tens of millions of retail traders already active on regulated platforms, many of whom have no access to perps today.
3. There are three retail markets at the scale that matters: the US, Europe and Asia. The US is the most contested, with many major exchanges and brokers competing for the same users and a long licensing path. Asia has high perps penetration but regulatory approaches vary by jurisdiction. Europe is where we are starting, and we will look at other regulated markets as and when it makes sense.
4. Regulated crypto derivatives in Europe have only recently expanded. Kraken, Coinbase and Bitstamp (owned by Robinhood) launched futures for EU clients over the past 18 months, each using regulatory infrastructure obtained through an acquisition of a licensed investment firm or exchange. That route is open to a handful of firms with the balance sheet for it, but for the far larger group of fintechs and brokers with users and no perps infrastructure, it is not. Our model is to offer builder codes on both venues: a way for partners to plug perps into their own apps, route users’ orders to the venue and earn a share of the fees. Self-custody wallets can integrate with the existing venue where available. Regulated brokers and fintechs will be able to use the regulated venue once it is live.
5. A regulated perps setup takes significant time and resources to build from scratch, and many fintechs lack the product and market expertise to run it well, starting with established market-maker relationships. For smaller players the economics may not work. For larger ones, regulated builder codes cut time to market, especially inside slow-moving large organisations, and deliver a quality product from day one.
6. The demand is clear. We are already in conversations with wallets, CFD brokers and fintechs across Europe, and we repeatedly hear the same request: a regulated venue with a broad range of crypto and RWA markets they can integrate.

Importantly, this does not change our DeFi offering or our commitment to the early community. The existing venue stays for crypto-native users where it is available. The regulated venue adds a new distribution channel and a new user base. 

Europe is the first step. Over time, we expect to replicate the same model in other markets, including the US. Our plan is subject to the relevant regulatory authorisations, and we will share specifics as they are confirmed. At a high level, we have an initial route to market, followed by a transition to our own licences.
