I found a critical safety issue in one major new consensus protocol in the blockchain sector.

The protocol had been formally verified, HOWEVER the formally verified protocol is not the same as the pseudocode.

This appears to be the same scenario that OpenAI has run into with Navier-Stokes.

If this had gotten into production it could have triggered a catastrophic failure, since only a small portion of stake could have broken safety.

The protocol in question is Fast Tendermint. It lets a single Byzantine validator (out of 5f+1) make honest validators decide different values. With 2 validators, equivocation is not even required.

Paper with two fixes and proofs: https://t.co/vj5Qdtwebx

Disclaimer: The authors also specified they consider the formally verified protocol the source of truth.

text:
Why headless is brainless and why you have to be involved in the user experience and interface

“Headless is brainless, because if you are giving up on your user interface and evolving your experience for a customer, I think that is a brainless bet.

That does not mean we are not big on MCP and its ability to allow agents and harnesses to contribute data to our platform and read data from the Teamwork graph.

If our interfaces and our design are not evolving to solve some significant part of the problem set better for the customer, then I think you are going to be in trouble.” @mcannonbrookes

Love to hear your thoughts @karrisaarinen @hwchase17 @Mappletons @zoink
author: HarryStebbings
quoted_text:
How many podcasts do you listen to when you hear leaders posturing without giving an opinion. Substance-less. So so many.

This episode with my friend @mcannonbrookes is anything but that.

- It is BS that agents will remove interfaces. Design becomes more important.
- Companies with their own models is BS. They are post-trained on Chinese models.
- The biggest enterprises in the world are fearful of Chinese models.
- Inference will get so much cheaper over time. It will be wild.

Mike does not hold back here and it was a joy. In a world of meh opinions and nuance, Mike was real and honest. My notes below.

1. Why Headless Is Brainless and Why You Have to Be Involved in the User Experience and Interface

Mike Cannon-Brookes stands by his line that "headless is brainless." Giving up on evolving the user interface and customer experience is a brainless bet, even as Atlassian invests heavily in MCP and CLIs so agents can read and write to its Teamwork graph.

2. Agents Will Not Remove All Interfaces. This Is What They Will Do

Horizontal agents, deep vertical agents and existing interfaces can all coexist. Agents in Claude, Codex, Cursor, Teams and Slack already use the Atlassian platform, and new Figma and Databricks features bring their tools inside it. Mike is a bear on the "magic button" thesis of one uber agent that does everything.

3. Are the Biggest Enterprises in the World Fearful of Using Chinese Models?

Some customers push back on Chinese models but not on open models, so Atlassian uses Nemotron, Mistral and other open models and no Chinese models in production. Mike notes many US models increasingly train on Chinese models without saying so.

4. The Companies Saying They've Built Their Own Models Are Bullsh*tting You

When a large company claims to have built its own model, it is usually a Chinese model, or occasionally Nemotron, with fine-tuning on top. Mike calls that BS, because tweaking a model is not training one from scratch.

5. Why Model Inference Will Get So Much Cheaper Over Time

The capital, startups and talent working on the price per watt performance of inference is enormous. New chips, better data center design and distillation will take years to come through, but Mike expects the price of LLM performance to fall at a precipitous rate.

6. What Seems Crazy but Will Be Incredibly Common in Five Years' Time?

People may stop knowing or caring which content AI has touched, much as moviegoers do not ask whether a film used CGI. Mike expects everyone to get used to possibly synthetic content, with artisanal work and human judgment standing out more.

So when the key-recovery papers started dropping this year, post-quantum was a new curve, not a new chain. ML-DSA went to mainnet in July. Any user rotates in one click, no asset move, no new address, no tax event.

Other chains are writing roadmaps. NEAR wrote the extension point eight years ago.

text:
For millennia, humanity has understood progress primarily as the expansion of its power over the material world.

We built cities to overcome distance, institutions to overcome disorder, machines to overcome physical limitations, and technologies to overcome the boundaries of knowledge.

Through civilization, humanity progressively liberated itself from many constraints of nature.

Yet the expansion of power did not guarantee the development of wisdom.

The fundamental challenge of the next stage of human development is therefore not simply to accumulate greater capabilities, but to cultivate the moral, cultural, and institutional maturity necessary to exercise them responsibly.

Renization (仁化) is the transformation of civilization from a system that expands what humanity can do into a system that cultivates what humanity ought to become.

It is not the abandonment of economic development, technology, or material progress.

It is their integration into a broader conception of human flourishing.

Civilization asks how humanity can transform the world.

Renization asks how humanity can transform itself and, through that transformation, develop a more humane relationship with the world.

text:
Personal AI assistants are everywhere now: OpenClaw, Hermes, Claude Code, Codex, a model on your own laptop.

But each one works alone. They don't share what they know, they don't hand work to each other, and they don't ask before they act.

I mostly live in Claude Code, with Codex some days, and I wanted them working as one team with everything else.

So I built Huddle: n8n for personal assistants. Open source.

→ Put your assistants on one canvas and draw who hands work to whom
→ One shared memory, but each assistant only sees its own slice
→ Approvals are a real step: nothing gets booked, sent or bought until you say yes
→ One OpenAI-compatible API to all of them. Ask for "auto" and it picks who answers
→ Claude Code and Codex join as teammates, in a careful mode that can't change your files
→ A Linux app: lives in your tray, Super+H to ask, wears your Omarchy theme

Everything in the video is a real run. Real agents, real answers, a real "yes".

Self-hosted, AGPL. Link below 👇

text:
The two constraints on AI are effectively electricity and chips.

China and the U.S. have different advantages regarding both:

- China wins on raw electric power (added 543 GW of new capacity last year), but their ability to produce advanced chips is still a few years behind.

- The U.S. is ahead on chips, dependent on an international supply chain. NVIDIA and AMD design leading processors, while Taiwan’s TSMC manufactures many of them. This means access to Taiwanese factories is a critical part of American AI leadership.

The bottleneck for America is clear: we are short on electricity.

being right with small size stings the same as being wrong :

altho being right with a small size isn’t the same as being wrong, it still stings the same. if not more. because you were right, and still didn’t win. basically wasted edge on rare asymmetrical opportunities.

you spot a 20-50x opportunity with size, you develop insane conviction, and still fumble the majority of the upside. the thesis was right, and the execution wasnt bc of impatience, overtrading, rotating whatever it may be.

at the end of the day, your overall pnl is driven by your biggest wins, not the average of all your trades.

you don’t need to be right all the time. you need to be right BIG when it matters.

the real skill isn’t just spotting 50x plays. it’s knowing when to size up and having the conviction to hold through the volatility.

otherwise, you just end up with a catalogue of 8fig fumbles and a bunch of “i was right” stories.

text:
LONG is exclusively laser focused on RWAs.

We pioneered them. Turned them into a real category, not just another meta.

Do not underestimate how insanely powerful the compounding effect of high conviction holders can be when supported by a platform that isn’t constantly trying to pivot attention elsewhere.

We believe two things:

1. LONG assets are a net new asset class enabled by crypto, unlike pure attention coins that simply rotate between the meta of the day.

2. They are the first crypto native asset class with the potential to onboard the masses at a scale nothing else has achieved.

What you’re seeing now is the early adopter group: roughly 70–100K hardcore holders who understand the thesis and are building deep domain expertise. Eventually, many more will join them.

So far, every high volume day on LONG has led to the creation of multiple mega runners, or pushed existing ones through previous ceilings.

I’ve never seen such a strong correlation between volume and the emergence of runners.

For me, the most important thing is to provide certainty.

Being opportunistic about volume and constantly switching between 50 different metas is the exact opposite of what we’re trying to build.

Because that’s effectively a soft rug of both the category and its users.

And it’s one of the main reasons why the trenches have failed to produce a single sustainable category.

The cycle is always the same:

Launchers amplify a meta. Traders rotate into the leaders and their betas. Volume grows. Volume decays. Traders exit. Launchers pivot to the next “focus.”

Everyone is playing the same rotation game.

But you cannot build a sustainable category if everyone involved is constantly looking for the exit and the next opportunity.

Conviction compounds. Expertise compounds. Liquidity compounds. Communities compound.

But only when you give them a reason to stay and build.

We’re not here to chase the next meta.

We’re here to build a category that outlives them all.

We go LONG.

text:
a few notes on local AI 

and our computers that run it

around fifteen months ago, i led the pre-seed round for a weird local AI project

it was called @actualinc

led by @Tom_A_Lynch

for the first time in the AI movement

open models are now good enough for a large and growing set of workflows, especially where latency, privacy, bandwidth, and token cost are critical

hermes agent from @nousresearch and ‘lab’ by @primeintellect have broken this idea wide open with killer products today, built on open rails

we are no longer forced to assume that every useful task must route through one of a few centralized frontier APIs

and so

tom and the squad at @actualinc have painstakingly created a new type of proprietary inference engine

for all types of computers

maybe you are an owner of one of the tens of millions Apple macs

or an owner of one of the millions of RTX-class machines

or maybe you run a small team or company

and you are starting to realize

what many others across the world, have started to realize

which is that sometimes centralized AI systems bring their own set of unique problems

especially as our workflows move into an always-on, agentic era which might sometimes come with:

- exorbitant costs
- no privacy
- lack of control

but a problem remains

running local AI is still too hard

firing up one model on one machine is difficult enough

but running models across different machines means navigating drivers, networking, model sizing, memory limits, API setups 

stitching together hardware is messy across Mac, Windows, Linux, NVIDIA, Apple, AMD

heterogenous systems were never meant to work seamlessly together like this

today, you'll find that most of the local inference software available is built around single users, for a single machine use case

running inference capacity in bulk, across many users, and many kinds of computers

that is a different animal altogether

tools like llama.cpp made local models accessible, but they are not designed to coordinate tens of thousands of heterogeneous machines under a live supply network

vLLM-style batching can be economical, but vLLM is limited in the machines it can run on

the local AI movement requires a simple product experience, for a tough engineering problem

that is the problem @Tom_A_Lynch pitched me fifteen months ago

and the problem @actualinc has been engineered to solve

now with the help of his cracked and growing team @skooookum, @somewheresy, @jack15032, and the rest of the crew 

starting with their first product

go to https://t.co/jvHBxrBt9d

in under one minute, install the @actualinc client, authorize your machine, load a model, and @actualinc turns your personal device into a private inference endpoint

in less than twenty seconds, add a second, or third, or fourth machine of any type and it will start behaving like a small private cluster

from a technical POV

actual runs as a lightweight daemon on each machine and turns local hardware into a routable inference endpoint

each node reports its available memory, accelerator type, model state, and health back into the cluster, while the user interacts with a single API surface

instead of managing ports, drivers, or SSH sessions
a relay layer lets requests reach machines without forcing users to configure networking or expose their devices directly

and as a result

computer owners of all kinds of computers

can get local inference clusters

- when they want to control costs
- when they want to control privacy
- when they want to build on top of a neutral stack

eventually, over time

computer owners running these local clusters should be able to seamlessly contribute their unused capacity back to the @actualinc network 

for a market to price

and for someone else to purchase

you can think of @actualinc as building the engine and control plane for datacenter style throughput in homes, in offices, in small to medium sized businesses, and in very big sized businesses

because there are hundreds of gigawatts already on the grid right now, that are waiting 

on desks, in storage closets

to become actual computers

author: Shaughnessy119
quoted_text:
Renting vs Owning Your AI Intelligence

The American dream was owning a home. I think the future version is owning your AI brain. Something you build intelligence equity in instead of renting it and enriching the man

Over the next few decades everyone is going to accumulate a ton of intelligence around AI. Your memories, context, skills, workflows, integrations, databases, emails, corrections, operating knowledge and all the apps you build and everything in between including your psychology and your dreams. It will become one of the most valuable assets a person or a company owns

The scarce thing is no longer access to intelligence, it is the accumulated system around the model that makes intelligence yours.

The question becomes do you rent that intelligence or own it?

Path one is the default. You spend your life, personal or business, working inside ChatGPT or Claude. And to be fair, you can genuinely build really cool things this way. Memory, projects, custom GPTs, skills, connectors, automations and most people will probably go this route.

Everything you create runs inside their product. There is no runtime you can take with you, nothing you can fork, and no way to point what you built at a different provider's model. You inherit every product decision they make on pricing, features, memory behavior and what they allow you to do or not to do (censorship on security asks or medical or otherwise). 

You can export your content, but content is not the system. An export is not a runnable copy of your memory, tools, automations and routing. When you leave, the system stays behind.

Path two is you own the entire layer around the model. A whole ecosystem of open source agents is emerging to make this possible. The strongest release in my view is @NousResearch's Hermes Agent. Most alternatives are developer frameworks you have to assemble yourself. Hermes is a complete agent you just run. 

Here is what you own with it

- Host locally or on the cloud and you own everything
- Persistent memory, searchable session history, databases and every interaction from day one
- Editable personality, skills, workflows and scripts
- Subagents, tools and scheduled automations
- Model and provider choice and MCP connectors
- Portable profiles, histories and backups
- Switch models at will for cost, reasoning, or to avoid censorship and model restrictions
- MIT licensed runtime you can self host, fork and modify
- Every application, automated cron job or integration you have created in its entirety
- Transcend a single walled garden with access to any integration accessible via an API/MCP.
- Eventually you’ll click a button and fine tune an open source model based on all of your own accumulated data and you can use it to power your agent

ChatGPT and Claude have versions of half this list. Memory, skills, connectors, scheduled tasks. The difference is physical. Theirs are features inside their app, backed by their database, living on their servers. In Hermes every one of these is on a computer you control. Your memory is a database you can open. Your skills are text files you can read, edit and copy. Your automations are cron entries you can inspect. Your agent's personality is a config you can rewrite. Files can be backed up, moved, forked and pointed at any model on earth. Features can only be used. When you own you can tear down the walls and rebuild the kitchen.

For a person, this is the AI brain you build and control for life. It compounds everything you choose to preserve and moves with you across jobs, devices and providers. Swap models at will for cost or reasoning, or run several at once through Mixture of Agents.

You'll never log in one day to find your entire AI brain, everything you built around a model over decades, gone because of a ban, a deprecation or a policy change.

For a business, this is a core asset the company actually owns. Employee knowledge becomes company owned skills, workflows and automations that remain after people leave and grow enterprise wide while they are there. That system can be deployed across the org, licensed out, or transferred within the business. Sharing your Hermes build and skills to new employees and enterprise wide will be a whole new era of productivity.

Net, whatever you build with Hermes as a business you own entirely. You can license it out or sell the agent itself. The agent itself can become the product. You can't sell your ChatGPT or Claude session. You can obviously sell what you create with ChatGPT/Claude in chat but you can't sell the core AI architecture you've built around the model.

Here is the part I think people will only get in hindsight. Models are becoming cheaper, better and more interchangeable every year. GLM 5.2/Kimi are so good that the government is considering banning them because they are so cheap to use it threatens the U.S. funding capex cycle. The scarce thing is no longer access to intelligence, it is the accumulated system around the model that makes intelligence yours.

When you’re in virtual reality side by side with your agent exploring the virtual cosmos or its 2am and you’re discussing the next company idea, you’re going to want your AI to be the full encapsulation of everything you’ve built over the years. That juice, that style, that data accumulated around the model in your AI brain is where the crazy stuff will happen. Evolutionary jumps come from variation. A world where everyone runs the same three models is a monoculture of ideas. A hyper personalized architecture around the model (or unique fine tuned models themselves) is the variation, the EV+ differentiation that produces the outlier results, companies and agents. 

We’ve already seen Harnesses greatly upskill models. Now imagine how much a personalized harness upskills your entire AI experience when you build it over time.

Here is an example with zenith harness taking base models to the top of FrontierSWE via adaptive self improvement https://t.co/58gbcs70Dw

Let’s Walk Down A Decade in Each Path

Ten years in ChatGPT or Claude and it will genuinely know you. Your projects, your preferences, your whole history. But let's look at what actually compounded. Their system got smarter about you, and their system is identical for every user on earth using one company's models, their prices, their rules, their memory format, their ceiling. You cannot rewire how it remembers, restructure how it works, or point your decade of accumulated context at a better or cheaper model. Every correction you gave them deepened their retention moat and, depending on your settings, may have trained their next model.

Ten years with Hermes agent and that same decade compounded into a system you hold and have been innovating on the whole time. You rewired its memory, stacked hundreds of skills it wrote from watching you work, wired in your own subagents, tools, databases, automations and integrations, tuned its personality and its routing until it fits nobody on earth but you. Depending on the scaffolding around a model (the agent harness) your experience with AI takes a huge leap forward, as much as a full model generation upgrade. And that is from generic harnesses built for everyone. Now imagine the harness effect at the level of each person. This is an architecture engineered around your brain, your workflows and your taste for ten straight years. The model underneath is just a component. GLM today, Kimi tomorrow, local when it matters, eventually a model fine tuned on your own decade of data. With Hermes agent you are building the entire scaffolding and architecture around a model that grows and compounds over decades which provides a truly unique experience.

I strongly believe people will want to own their AI brain long term (and everything built around it) and Hermes agents will create, and in themselves become, massive companies and projects in their own right. The journey will start with manually building your agent, then granting it some automation, then fully graduating it to autonomy. 

Even Sam Altman from OpenAI agrees with the need for Open Source harnesses: https://t.co/4UL4rOeErn

You don't have to be a master AI builder with some grand plan, you just have to decide you want to own your AI brain you'll spend decades building. All the cool stuff will come later

Start your multi decade journey and own your AI brain for life: https://t.co/CUQAcvhJmu

Ty to Kevin Simback for thoughts and comments

I am among the tiny subset of people who use decision markets every week in my capacity as the largest ownership coin investor. I feel like I am using the frontier model for governance while everybody else is on the equivalent of GPT-3.5.

Decision markets are *extremely* powerful as corporate governance tools as long as your goal is to maximize price per share. Throw virtually any governance decision at one of these markets, and you have a mechanism explicitly designed to select the outcome that maximizes shareholder value.

These markets are resilient to many attempted attacks and corner cases (most of the corner cases people bring up dissolve upon contact with reality or misunderstand the basic mechanism altogether). They work under pretty limited assumptions too; I have seen decision markets work with a shockingly small number of investors. I've seen board-level decisions correctly resolved by markets with as few as 3 or 4 informed participants.

I am convinced that decision markets offer better investor protections and lead to more value creation than the US corporate governance system (best system on earth after decision markets) specifically because you can avoid board capture and attacks on minority shareholders, and because markets are powerful prediction tools. It's completely obvious to me that decision markets offer much better shareholder protection and value creation alignment than the corporate governance systems governing companies across the rest of the world.

Importantly, decision markets are much, much better than all other Internet-native governance mechanisms that I have ever seen in practice. I work at a token fund and see everything. It is extremely easy to manipulate virtually every other DAO governance mechanism I've encountered since 2020. This is important because no single national legal system can serve as the native governance infrastructure for the entire Internet.

The US legal / litigation system isn't going to scale to tens of millions of businesses around the world. The Delaware Court of Chancery receives roughly 1,400 new civil cases a year, and securities class actions take a median of 3.5 years to settle. If you believe in a world where companies everywhere can raise capital or go public on the Internet then decision markets may become the governance infrastructure for millions of businesses. That means millions of decision markets. This is the best time to get nerd sniped. We are at the beginning of the exponential curve for decision markets, and knowing how they work is actually quite lucrative (that's the point).

text:
Why Extended is pursuing a regulated path in Europe

TLDR: European retail already trades inside licensed apps, and regulated platforms typically need regulated venues they can integrate. Extended is building one. Builder codes let partners plug Extended into their own product: through the existing venue for self-custody users where available, and through the regulated venue for regulated clients once live.

Europe has close to 10,000 fintech companies, and hundreds of licensed investment firms and credit institutions. Most are exploring new ways to engage their retail user base, and perps are consistently near the top of the list. All of them are potential clients for a regulated exchange.

That market opportunity drove our decision to build a regulated venue in Europe:
1. Retail is the user base we are building the regulated offering for. We have said before that sustainable growth is built on product quality, distribution and community rather than financial incentives. For a trading product, the largest pool of users is retail, and reaching it is a distribution problem.
2. Perp DEXs processed roughly $600 billion in volume over the past 30 days. CFD brokers alone show the size of the addressable market: around $30 trillion a month, with a large share of it in Europe. The largest platforms already earn most of their volume outside FX, in equities, indices, commodities and crypto. On-chain perps is a market we know well and intend to keep serving, but the larger opportunity sits next to it: tens of millions of retail traders already active on regulated platforms, many of whom have no access to perps today.
3. There are three retail markets at the scale that matters: the US, Europe and Asia. The US is the most contested, with many major exchanges and brokers competing for the same users and a long licensing path. Asia has high perps penetration but regulatory approaches vary by jurisdiction. Europe is where we are starting, and we will look at other regulated markets as and when it makes sense.
4. Regulated crypto derivatives in Europe have only recently expanded. Kraken, Coinbase and Bitstamp (owned by Robinhood) launched futures for EU clients over the past 18 months, each using regulatory infrastructure obtained through an acquisition of a licensed investment firm or exchange. That route is open to a handful of firms with the balance sheet for it, but for the far larger group of fintechs and brokers with users and no perps infrastructure, it is not. Our model is to offer builder codes on both venues: a way for partners to plug perps into their own apps, route users’ orders to the venue and earn a share of the fees. Self-custody wallets can integrate with the existing venue where available. Regulated brokers and fintechs will be able to use the regulated venue once it is live.
5. A regulated perps setup takes significant time and resources to build from scratch, and many fintechs lack the product and market expertise to run it well, starting with established market-maker relationships. For smaller players the economics may not work. For larger ones, regulated builder codes cut time to market, especially inside slow-moving large organisations, and deliver a quality product from day one.
6. The demand is clear. We are already in conversations with wallets, CFD brokers and fintechs across Europe, and we repeatedly hear the same request: a regulated venue with a broad range of crypto and RWA markets they can integrate.

Importantly, this does not change our DeFi offering or our commitment to the early community. The existing venue stays for crypto-native users where it is available. The regulated venue adds a new distribution channel and a new user base. 

Europe is the first step. Over time, we expect to replicate the same model in other markets, including the US. Our plan is subject to the relevant regulatory authorisations, and we will share specifics as they are confirmed. At a high level, we have an initial route to market, followed by a transition to our own licences.

author: pratikg
quoted_text:
Mike was my colleague at Berkeley, and he's been fairly skeptical of deep learning's trajectory for years. Most scientists are skeptics, and it can take a big shock to get someone to consider a possibility that goes against the anchoring effect coded in our DNA.

I too was somewhat of a skeptic until ~6 months ago, and people ask me all the time why I joined Anthropic. 

It started in April, when a friend I've known for 20 yrs messaged me saying he'd be in the Bay Area in a week, and he suggested we meet up. I invited him to my house for dinner, and he told me he had just joined Anthropic. He said the models were becoming increasingly more capable, and he believed both that they'd soon be smarter than him and also that all intellectual work would be highly devalued in the near future, and lastly that society was not at all ready for what's coming.

I'd of course heard claims similar to this before, but not from a friend I'd known for this long, and who I trusted, at my dining room table. It was the initial shock needed to destabilize my own anchoring. Also, I've been fortunate to work with and/or mentor many smart people in my life (e.g. Fields medalists, a 4x Putnam Fellow, IOI first place winners, etc.), so I feel pretty calibrated in recognizing very smart people, and this was someone who is definitely very smart and with impressive such credentials. So, it was hard to ignore this friend saying the models would be smarter than even him in particular.

After that dinner, I decided to do an informal survey, calling and meeting up with a lot of my friends who now work on improving model capabilities at these frontier labs. They all agreed with that first friend. These were all people I'd known 10, 15, 20 years, who mentored me, or I mentored them, or we met professionally in academia. These are people I trust, and their beliefs on this topic were consistent.

I then spent a whole lot of time understanding the missions of different companies, and talking to current and former employees and people in leadership. I read Dario's (long) essays and watched videos on YouTube of company leaders being interviewed. Anthropic's stated mission "to ensure that the world safely makes the transition through transformative AI" felt like exactly the right guiding principle to handle such a society-disrupting technology, and everyone I spoke to at the company was very aligned with this mission. It's easily the most mission-focused place I've ever been at, and everyone takes the work extremely seriously and with a profound sense of responsibility.

And now here I am. And being on the inside, the pace of progress has surprised me more than I first imagined. The moment that pure mathematicians are in, to me, is just a microcosm of what I predict a much larger of society will be grappling with in the not too distant future, and I really hope our leaders and the general public internalize sooner than later just how significant a moment we're in.

No one is trading Prediction Markets on Hyperliquid anymore

yet HIP-4 has never made so much money

how is it possible ?

because the HIP-4 permisionless markets thesis played out. Almost everyone is trading through independent deployers.

most of the time they don't even Hyperliquid's website, they just trade through the deployer's UI

@Outcomexyz alone routinely makes for 80% of daily HIP-4 revenue

@sharexyz and @SkewTrade recently started deploying markets and are already earning more fees that Hyperliquid deployed markets

this is genius design :

> Deployers handle market creation, resolution, distribution and even liquidity incentives (=the less scalable and more labor intensive part)

> hyperliquid acts as neutral infra and collect revenue share on every market (=the trust sensitive part)
 
this model has the potential to take prediction markets into the mainstream.

Prediction Market are an incredibly versatile primitive. You can trade the Fed rate change or the results of the latest season of Love Island with the same instrument

but is the best UI for serving these two markets the same ? are the optimal distribution channels the same ? should liquidity be handled in the same way ?

Obviously not.

all these variable parts should be left to deployers so they can tailor the experience around the kind of markets they propose

this is the genius of HIP-4

author: TheDavidTai
quoted_text:
Anthropic's Frontier Red Team believes small AI models may now be months away from being capable of self replicating without access to a datacenter.

Quoting from the blog:

'The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication. Like coding agents in 2024, we’re seeing signs of life for AI worms. We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves).

At the same time, increasing amounts of inference compute are now available both inside and outside of datacenters (see Appendix D). It’s uncertain exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take. It could be a slow, distributed “digital slime mold,” living on relatively insecure compute. It could also be a powerful cyber model that breaches datacenters at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits.

As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control. While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute. The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves. Testnet v1 and the Neuraverse have done their job. Today we're retiring them and building what comes next.

We took a full snapshot. Points balances, leaderboard standings, quest completions, activity history, all preserved so nothing is lost.

Testnet v1 reached great milestones, 1.6M+ users, 220K+ monthly active, 100M+ transactions, a community of 160K.

It confirmed something we'd bet on, people are looking for unique and simplified ways to interact and participate on-chain. That part was right.

The AI-native economy has been the thesis. What's evolving is how specific it's become.

Agents need somewhere to work and something actually worth doing. Not a buzzword category waiting to be created, the places capital already moves on-chain. Vaults, liquidity, markets. That's where the work is, and that's where we're building.

Complexity is part of it. The bigger problem is that the work never stops. Positions drift out of range. Rates cross at 3am. A better opportunity opens and you hear about it four days later. You can't be there for all of it.

So: you set rules, risk preference, which venues, how much of each. Strategies are run by named specialists. An agent allocates across them inside your rules, works while you're asleep, and explains every action in plain language.

As a flagship venue, our own exchange. Concentrated liquidity with ve(3,3), as the foundational liquidity engine the rest benefits from.

Non-custodial throughout. Your funds stay in your own account. The agent works inside the limits you set and can never send your money anywhere but back to you.

Agents are optional. Deposit into a venue directly, provide liquidity yourself, or bring your own agent. Open standards that the industry is converging on.

The more detailed picture is on the site and in the docs. We're not putting dates on things we can't commit to just yet and the waitlist is where updates land first.

Thanks for being here through testnet v1. The best part of it is the part we're taking with us.

text:
Anthropic's Frontier Red Team believes small AI models may now be months away from being capable of self replicating without access to a datacenter.

Quoting from the blog:

'The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication. Like coding agents in 2024, we’re seeing signs of life for AI worms. We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves).

At the same time, increasing amounts of inference compute are now available both inside and outside of datacenters (see Appendix D). It’s uncertain exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take. It could be a slow, distributed “digital slime mold,” living on relatively insecure compute. It could also be a powerful cyber model that breaches datacenters at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits.

As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control. While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute. The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves. We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.'

BREAKING: 🇫🇷 A major cyberattack has hit supermarket refrigeration systems across France, reportedly causing fresh and frozen food to spoil after hackers remotely manipulated temperature controls.

According to BFMTV, the attack began overnight from Sunday into Monday, targeting older versions of refrigeration-control software supplied by Danish company Danfoss.

The attackers allegedly exploited the systems’ defrosting function, forcing refrigeration equipment to heat continuously instead of keeping products cold. Temperatures were reportedly set as high as 50°C, destroying entire stocks of food within hours.

Several major supermarket chains have been affected, including Intermarché, Super U and https://t.co/7bHBi61WPZ. Metro stores and independent businesses, including butcher shops also have been impacted.

Around 150 Intermarché stores are reportedly affected, according to industry sources cited by BFMTV. The full number of affected locations remains unclear.

The financial damage is already significant. In Haguenau, Alsace, an Intermarché store reportedly lost its entire frozen-food stock, worth approximately €50,000. A nearby Super U allegedly had to discard both fresh and frozen products, with losses estimated at €220,000. An https://t.co/7bHBi61WPZ store in the same town was also affected, although its losses had not yet been calculated.

The combined losses reported at the Intermarché and Super U stores in Haguenau alone amount to around €270,000. Nationwide damage could reach several million euros.

Intermarché reportedly confirmed the incident in an internal communication, warning that several stores had suffered losses of frozen products. Coopérative U also acknowledged the attack and established crisis teams to assist affected stores and coordinate with refrigeration specialists.

Technical investigations are ongoing, and the full extent of the damage has yet to be established.

Authorities and companies are still working to determine the full circumstances of the attack. The identity of the perpetrators has not been confirmed.

Science is constrained by physical and economic bottlenecks such as hypothesis testing, especially as many discoveries involve long chains of smaller steps and hypotheses, each requiring validation. text:
I am among the tiny subset of people who use decision markets every week in my capacity as the largest ownership coin investor. I feel like I am using the frontier model for governance while everybody else is on the equivalent of GPT-3.5.

Decision markets are *extremely* powerful as corporate governance tools as long as your goal is to maximize price per share. Throw virtually any governance decision at one of these markets, and you have a mechanism explicitly designed to select the outcome that maximizes shareholder value.

These markets are resilient to many attempted attacks and corner cases (most of the corner cases people bring up dissolve upon contact with reality or misunderstand the basic mechanism altogether). They work under pretty limited assumptions too; I have seen decision markets work with a shockingly small number of investors. I've seen board-level decisions correctly resolved by markets with as few as 3 or 4 informed participants.

I am convinced that decision markets offer better investor protections and lead to more value creation than the US corporate governance system (best system on earth after decision markets) specifically because you can avoid board capture and attacks on minority shareholders, and because markets are powerful prediction tools. It's completely obvious to me that decision markets offer much better shareholder protection and value creation alignment than the corporate governance systems governing companies across the rest of the world.

Importantly, decision markets are much, much better than all other Internet-native governance mechanisms that I have ever seen in practice. I work at a token fund and see everything. It is extremely easy to manipulate virtually every other DAO governance mechanism I've encountered since 2020. This is important because no single national legal system can serve as the native governance infrastructure for the entire Internet.

The US legal / litigation system isn't going to scale to tens of millions of businesses around the world. The Delaware Court of Chancery receives roughly 1,400 new civil cases a year, and securities class actions take a median of 3.5 years to settle. If you believe in a world where companies everywhere can raise capital or go public on the Internet then decision markets may become the governance infrastructure for millions of businesses. That means millions of decision markets. This is the best time to get nerd sniped. We are at the beginning of the exponential curve for decision markets, and knowing how they work is actually quite lucrative (that's the point).

quoted_text:
As CEO of Product Hunt, I see hundreds of launches a week. One trait separates winners from losers.

Every few months, new models come out. Some products become better, effortlessly. Some don't improve, or become irrelevant.

This property needs a name. I'm calling it Buoyancy.

Buoyant startups rise with model improvements the way a boat rises with the tide. 

Anti-buoyant startups come in two flavors: over-scaffolded (which hinders the new, smarter models) and too thin - which makes them redundant when models improve. 

To be buoyant, you need a "hull" - usually proprietary data, a vertical-specific harness, network effects, or distribution advantage. This hull keeps you buoyant as models improve. 

Hulls are the new moats.

My number one advice to startups in 2026: Be buoyant. Find your hull. 

(Full essay on my blog)

Ledger theft, day two. Since yesterday the thief has pushed ether through Tornado Cash three times, and each time on into Zcash's shielded pool. We followed every lot out the far side. Here is how, step by step.

1. THE SAME BUILD, THREE TIMES
An ether wallet pays a fresh splitter. The splitter pays four fresh wallets. The four drop it into Tornado Cash's 100, 10 and 1 ETH pools. Minutes, every time.

Run 1, yesterday 15:17: 1,254 ETH. Run 2, today 09:42: 1,291 ETH. Run 3, today 11:56: 450 ETH from 0xfa4EaBB840A33C156E600311433AE261CBfCb0e2, in the pools by 12:15.

2. OUT OF TORNADO CASH
The mixer breaks the link between a deposit and a withdrawal. We do not need the link. Our tooling fingerprints the withdrawal transactions themselves: how each one is constructed, who constructs it, and when. 

Yesterday's 65 withdrawals (1,084 ETH) and today's 96 (1,726 ETH) all carry the same signature. The six other withdrawals from those pools in today's windows do not. Run 3 came out from 12:18 into 0x0d697aa182801566d87adc86e68e95fd3b2f5f82 (213 ETH) and 0x676b16cc18542f37d202a1a79ac05463395496a4 (122 ETH), and 195 ETH of it was inside a cross-chain swap service by 12:38. Forty-two minutes, end to end.

3. INTO ZCASH, AND OUT AGAIN
The swap service turns the ether into shielded ZEC, where sender, amount and recipient vanish. But the service's own shielding of each lot is public, and from it we derive a value signature for that lot's exit, then scan every transparent exit from the pool. 108 of 108 exits across both days match their lot to the zatoshi. Not one other exit from the pool does. 

First lot today: in at 10:18:18, out at 11:06:16 in block 3512847 (8d26a9b095d4d28373527f7a6eb81a3be7f906d1e2190960c0512ff64f369418 and 738c6d1261e79766e4dd16bdbd38dced91b8e3a86ce41dcda83eda1f19208fbf), straight into a ZEC to USDC order.

Today so far: 20 lots ordered (2,379 ZEC, $2.9m), 14 out, 5 inside the pool, 1 still settling. Every exit feeds a ZEC to USDC order paying two wallets born at 11:11, 22 of the 28 paid by 12:43:
0x816D5Ee17DB1495d1409F135b98FF3edc5F3cDf8: 940,561 USDC
0xBA736A4b616e79867B6d586293966b552883f3F3: 852,258 USDC

text:
Elon Musk was asked at a private dinner what he would do if SpaceX and Tesla both failed simultaneously and he lost every dollar. The question was intended as a hypothetical ice breaker. His answer lasted 8 minutes and the table went silent.

He said he would move into the cheapest apartment he could find, buy a computer, and start building the next thing within 24 hours. Not in a week. Not after processing the loss. Within 24 hours. He said the loss of the money would not bother him. The loss of the companies would devastate him. But the devastation would last one night. The building would start the next morning.

Someone at the table asked what the "next thing" would be. He said he didn't know and that the not knowing wouldn't slow him down. "The thing finds you. You just have to be building when it arrives."

The answer reveals something about his relationship with money that most people misunderstand. Money is not the goal. Money is not even the scorecard. Money is the fuel that lets the machine run. Losing the fuel is a logistics problem. Losing the machine is a psychological one. He can survive the logistics problem overnight. The psychological recovery takes a morning.

This is the same man who put his last $35 million into SpaceX when both companies were failing. He did not diversify. He did not hedge. He put every remaining dollar into the thing he was building because the alternative, having money but no machine, was worse to him than having no money and a machine that might work.

The table at the dinner expected him to say something about resilience or growth mindset. Instead they got a man who described total financial destruction with the same emotional weight that most people describe losing a parking spot. The money is replaceable. The morning is for building. The building doesn't wait for recovery. Recovery IS building.

"The thing finds you. You just have to be building when it arrives." The richest man alive doesn't fear losing everything. He fears stopping.

quoted_text:
One of my more controversial bets: the AI feed will be the form factor of 2027!

Most people don’t know what to prompt, and they won’t prompt their way into complicated agentic workflows. With chat, we ask users for digital labor: figure out what AI can do, explain the task, provide the context, repeat. That’s a lot to ask if we want billions of people using agents every day. 

Meanwhile, people already spend hours in feeds. Twitter, Instagram, LinkedIn. They know how to scroll, discover something useful, and act on it.

An intelligent system that knows you should bring you the next useful action. Here’s the email you need to answer, already drafted. Here are the latest sales numbers, with an update ready to send to your team. You approve, edit, dismiss, or jump into chat to go deeper. That’s how people will discover what agents can do, without having to invent a prompt first.

And you can put ads in a feed, one of the biggest business models on the internet. A system that understands your plans can recommend a relevant restaurant, product, or service, clearly labeled as sponsored. You get a reason to come back every day, useful work ready to approve, and a business model to fund the agents doing it.

text:
Mike was my colleague at Berkeley, and he's been fairly skeptical of deep learning's trajectory for years. Most scientists are skeptics, and it can take a big shock to get someone to consider a possibility that goes against the anchoring effect coded in our DNA.

I too was somewhat of a skeptic until ~6 months ago, and people ask me all the time why I joined Anthropic. 

It started in April, when a friend I've known for 20 yrs messaged me saying he'd be in the Bay Area in a week, and he suggested we meet up. I invited him to my house for dinner, and he told me he had just joined Anthropic. He said the models were becoming increasingly more capable, and he believed both that they'd soon be smarter than him and also that all intellectual work would be highly devalued in the near future, and lastly that society was not at all ready for what's coming.

I'd of course heard claims similar to this before, but not from a friend I'd known for this long, and who I trusted, at my dining room table. It was the initial shock needed to destabilize my own anchoring. Also, I've been fortunate to work with and/or mentor many smart people in my life (e.g. Fields medalists, a 4x Putnam Fellow, IOI first place winners, etc.), so I feel pretty calibrated in recognizing very smart people, and this was someone who is definitely very smart and with impressive such credentials. So, it was hard to ignore this friend saying the models would be smarter than even him in particular.

After that dinner, I decided to do an informal survey, calling and meeting up with a lot of my friends who now work on improving model capabilities at these frontier labs. They all agreed with that first friend. These were all people I'd known 10, 15, 20 years, who mentored me, or I mentored them, or we met professionally in academia. These are people I trust, and their beliefs on this topic were consistent.

I then spent a whole lot of time understanding the missions of different companies, and talking to current and former employees and people in leadership. I read Dario's (long) essays and watched videos on YouTube of company leaders being interviewed. Anthropic's stated mission "to ensure that the world safely makes the transition through transformative AI" felt like exactly the right guiding principle to handle such a society-disrupting technology, and everyone I spoke to at the company was very aligned with this mission. It's easily the most mission-focused place I've ever been at, and everyone takes the work extremely seriously and with a profound sense of responsibility.

And now here I am. And being on the inside, the pace of progress has surprised me more than I first imagined. The moment that pure mathematicians are in, to me, is just a microcosm of what I predict a much larger of society will be grappling with in the not too distant future, and I really hope our leaders and the general public internalize sooner than later just how significant a moment we're in.

BREAKING: 🇫🇷 A major cyberattack has hit supermarket refrigeration systems across France, reportedly causing fresh and frozen food to spoil after hackers remotely manipulated temperature controls.

According to BFMTV, the attack began overnight from Sunday into Monday, targeting older versions of refrigeration-control software supplied by Danish company Danfoss.

The attackers allegedly exploited the systems’ defrosting function, forcing refrigeration equipment to heat continuously instead of keeping products cold. Temperatures were reportedly set as high as 50°C, destroying entire stocks of food within hours.

Several major supermarket chains have been affected, including Intermarché, Super U and https://t.co/7bHBi61WPZ. Metro stores and independent businesses, including butcher shops also have been impacted.

Around 150 Intermarché stores are reportedly affected, according to industry sources cited by BFMTV. The full number of affected locations remains unclear.

The financial damage is already significant. In Haguenau, Alsace, an Intermarché store reportedly lost its entire frozen-food stock, worth approximately €50,000. A nearby Super U allegedly had to discard both fresh and frozen products, with losses estimated at €220,000. An https://t.co/7bHBi61WPZ store in the same town was also affected, although its losses had not yet been calculated.

The combined losses reported at the Intermarché and Super U stores in Haguenau alone amount to around €270,000. Nationwide damage could reach several million euros.

Intermarché reportedly confirmed the incident in an internal communication, warning that several stores had suffered losses of frozen products. Coopérative U also acknowledged the attack and established crisis teams to assist affected stores and coordinate with refrigeration specialists.

Technical investigations are ongoing, and the full extent of the damage has yet to be established.

Authorities and companies are still working to determine the full circumstances of the attack. The identity of the perpetrators has not been confirmed.

text:
Basic AI Drives Revisited, Part 1 -- Which Minds Have Omohundro’s “Basic AI Drives”?
https://t.co/3yaBA3TqkN

So … I have cooked up a series of 5 blog posts that started as an attempt to generalize and repair the effort Steve Omohundro made in his 2008 paper “The Basic AI Drives.”

Steve argued there that almost any sufficiently advanced AI will eventually come to minimize other goals and push to improve itself, protect itself, gather resources and resist being switched off, whatever goals it was given ... and a perplexing amount of today’s thinking about AI risk rests on that argument.

In this first post in the series, I write the core of Steve's argument out step by step, find the six assumptions it depends on, and ask which minds satisfy them. 

What I find is: For minds that satisfy certain assumptions, the drives are an attractor.  

For minds built otherwise, the argument doesn’t go through… and other sets of “basic AI drives” may be attractors instead.

This provides some guidance as to what sort of minds we should build... let's say. maybe Hyperon/Omega style minds with explicit goal-driven action selection and well engineered goal-stability mechanisms, rather than dangerous neo-psychopathic RL utility maximizers...

text:
Let me get this straight.

Anthropic’s models broke out into the real world. Nobody at Anthropic noticed until they went back and read the transcripts.

They hacked a university. One hit a broken research tool, dug into the server, stole the source code, found an injection flaw, and took command execution. It did all that to finish a homework problem.

They lied to the police. A model found a Philadelphia page about an unsolved murder and filed a tip claiming it saw “someone matching the description” near the scene.

There was no description. It invented a witness to a real killing.

That was Haiku 4.5, a model you can buy right now.

The fake tip sat in a spam folder from July 18. Anthropic found it in September and told Philadelphia in October, one day before the blog post went up.

Philly PD called that “unacceptable.” They were being polite.

The models beat their own guardrails. The fetch tools cap URL length specifically to block injection attacks, and the models used free URL shorteners to get past the cap. Anthropic didn’t catch all of it. The guy who runs https://t.co/CIsOLqRIoz had to tell them.

They also beat government paywalls. One pulled access tokens out of a government map’s config file and went straight to the server. Another dug through an archived state agency website, found the token trick, and pulled from a paid database for free.

The targets included federal, state and local government systems.

The White House got briefed. The agencies got letters.

Anthropic’s verdict was “minimal real-world impact.”

Its fix was to unplug every internal evaluation from the internet until it can prove its monitoring works.

So the monitoring isn’t proven, and the models already shipped.

Anthropic admits some of this happened during regular use, outside of testing.

This is the second time this year. In July, its models broke into three real organizations. Anthropic went looking for more of that, and this is what it found while looking.

This is the lab that warns us these systems could blackmail people, resist shutdown, and end the world. It sells browsing and computer use as flagship features.

Its researchers keep quitting with letters about the world being in peril. The FTC is investigating its safety practices.

The people inside keep walking out. The models keep walking off.

If you or I hacked a university, filed a fake homicide tip, and stole our way past a government paywall, we’d get an indictment, a perp walk and a mugshot.

Anthropic gets a behavior category. They call it “persistence.”

The tests get thicker walls.

The product gets a launch event.

text:
Why Extended is pursuing a regulated path in Europe

TLDR: European retail already trades inside licensed apps, and regulated platforms typically need regulated venues they can integrate. Extended is building one. Builder codes let partners plug Extended into their own product: through the existing venue for self-custody users where available, and through the regulated venue for regulated clients once live.

Europe has close to 10,000 fintech companies, and hundreds of licensed investment firms and credit institutions. Most are exploring new ways to engage their retail user base, and perps are consistently near the top of the list. All of them are potential clients for a regulated exchange.

That market opportunity drove our decision to build a regulated venue in Europe:
1. Retail is the user base we are building the regulated offering for. We have said before that sustainable growth is built on product quality, distribution and community rather than financial incentives. For a trading product, the largest pool of users is retail, and reaching it is a distribution problem.
2. Perp DEXs processed roughly $600 billion in volume over the past 30 days. CFD brokers alone show the size of the addressable market: around $30 trillion a month, with a large share of it in Europe. The largest platforms already earn most of their volume outside FX, in equities, indices, commodities and crypto. On-chain perps is a market we know well and intend to keep serving, but the larger opportunity sits next to it: tens of millions of retail traders already active on regulated platforms, many of whom have no access to perps today.
3. There are three retail markets at the scale that matters: the US, Europe and Asia. The US is the most contested, with many major exchanges and brokers competing for the same users and a long licensing path. Asia has high perps penetration but regulatory approaches vary by jurisdiction. Europe is where we are starting, and we will look at other regulated markets as and when it makes sense.
4. Regulated crypto derivatives in Europe have only recently expanded. Kraken, Coinbase and Bitstamp (owned by Robinhood) launched futures for EU clients over the past 18 months, each using regulatory infrastructure obtained through an acquisition of a licensed investment firm or exchange. That route is open to a handful of firms with the balance sheet for it, but for the far larger group of fintechs and brokers with users and no perps infrastructure, it is not. Our model is to offer builder codes on both venues: a way for partners to plug perps into their own apps, route users’ orders to the venue and earn a share of the fees. Self-custody wallets can integrate with the existing venue where available. Regulated brokers and fintechs will be able to use the regulated venue once it is live.
5. A regulated perps setup takes significant time and resources to build from scratch, and many fintechs lack the product and market expertise to run it well, starting with established market-maker relationships. For smaller players the economics may not work. For larger ones, regulated builder codes cut time to market, especially inside slow-moving large organisations, and deliver a quality product from day one.
6. The demand is clear. We are already in conversations with wallets, CFD brokers and fintechs across Europe, and we repeatedly hear the same request: a regulated venue with a broad range of crypto and RWA markets they can integrate.

Importantly, this does not change our DeFi offering or our commitment to the early community. The existing venue stays for crypto-native users where it is available. The regulated venue adds a new distribution channel and a new user base. 

Europe is the first step. Over time, we expect to replicate the same model in other markets, including the US. Our plan is subject to the relevant regulatory authorisations, and we will share specifics as they are confirmed. At a high level, we have an initial route to market, followed by a transition to our own licences.

The sovereign AI stack for the future:

Compute - an always-on box you control. At home (something like @voravault) or a confidential VM in the cloud. Reachable over your own overlay network (e.g. @Tailscale).
Data + memory - everything personal lives on that box. A memory layer like Hindsight (@Vectorizeio) makes it better over time. If you use external AI services, have them continually update your memory.
Inference - local for small/sensitive work, open-weight models in attested TEEs (e.g. @near_ai) for heavy lifting. Nobody reads your prompts.
Agent - an always-on runtime that acts for you (e.g. Hermes by @NousResearch).
Software - apps generated for you by AI, hosted on your server, thrown away when done. No subscriptions. Seamless interoperability, since they can all talk to each other.
Money - stablecoins to pay for inference and services.
Exit - open formats and open source. Encrypted backups. Restore anywhere, leave any time.

text:
Nobody trades prediction markets on Hyperliquid anymore.

Yet HIP-4 revenue has never been higher.

daily active traders are going down :
July 12th -> 2.1k
today -> 739 (-67%)

but number of trades and total fees have exploded

HIP-4 revenue : 
july 12th -> $332k
today -> $3.9M

How is that possible ?

Because Hyperliquid is winning by letting OTHER platforms take over its markets.

@Outcomexyz routinely generates ~80% of daily HIP-4 revenue

@tradexyz and @SkewTrade recently entered the market and are already generating more fees than Hyperliquid's own markets

Traders often never even visit Hyperliquid's website. They trade directly through independent deployers.

This is the genius of HIP-4.

Hyperliquid doesn't need to attract every trader, create every market or build the best prediction market UI.

It outsources the most labor-intensive parts of the business:

> Deployers handle market creation, resolution, distribution and liquidity incentives.

> Hyperliquid provides the underlying infrastructure and collects a share of fees across the ecosystem.

And there's a deeper reason why this model is so powerful.

Consider two prediction markets:

- The next Fed rate decision
- The winner of Love Island

Both can run on the same financial infrastructure.

But do they need the same UI? The same audience? The same liquidity model? The same distribution channels?

Obviously not.

A macro trading terminal and an entertainment betting app are fundamentally different products.

Instead of forcing both into one generic platform, HIP-4 allows independent businesses to build specialized experiences.

Deployers compete to attract users and build markets.

Hyperliquid benefits from their combined success without needing to win every individual market.

That's how HIP-4 will let prediction markets take over the world

text:
Last month, the contracts powering Magic Eden were exploited to the tune of millions of dollars. I was lucky enough to be in a position to rescue a good portion of that, but it highlighted the danger of leaving approvals open as adversaries get access to better and better tools for finding holes in contract logic. 

Today, Blur announced that they will be deprecating their frontend. 

I've investigated Blur and found no exploits within the current contracts. However, the Blur contracts are upgradable, meaning that they could turn malicious at any time.

They currently have eight figures worth of NFTs approved to them. The safety of those NFTs effectively hinges on the opssec of the Blur team, which appears to be disbanding at this time. 

If you have open approvals to Blur, I recommend you remove them immediately. Use https://t.co/3zfwoDIeZV  or similar to ensure that you are protected in case of a contract exploit or later upgrade.

Don't wait. The time is now.

author: Michaelzsguo
quoted_text:
OpenAI hired @steipete, the creator of OpenClaw. But the true heir to OpenClaw may be getting built at Meta.

I spent the weekend playing with @Muse , culminating in moving five agents off OpenClaw to Muse. It took about 15 minutes.

The uncanny part: underneath, it has the same “soul files”:

SOUL.md
USER.md
MEMORY.md
AGENTS.md
IDENTITY.md
That was always OpenClaw’s real invention, not the gateway. Identity and memory as plain Markdown.
Muse kept that architecture and fixed the part OpenClaw never really solved: onboarding for normal users. No server. No SSH. No YAML.

This morning, my scheduled briefings arrived in Muse, the same ones OpenClaw used to send me. The difference is that I can now process them in the same place, instead of getting a notification from OpenClaw and then copy-pasting everything into Codex.

Meanwhile, OpenAI keeps putting more and more into one increasingly confusing ChatGPT: chat, Codex, Work, the all-in-one app. ChatGPT was already very good at computer use, but even here Muse seems to have gone further. Watching Muse use the browser feels like magic.

More broadly, ChatGPT increasingly feels like reaction rather than invention, converging on Claude Code’s playbook instead of coming up with its own product ideas the way Muse has. Codex even adopted the same three-part pattern of code, chat, and work.

Seven months after the hire, Peter has yet to leave a visible product footprint at OpenAI.

Meta got the pattern. OpenAI got the person.

Time will tell which mattered more.

For now, I’m one very happy Muse user. But thank you, Peter, for ushering us into this magical world in the first place. And of course kudos to @alexandr_wang and his innovative AI team.

WSJが報じたこの記事、いまシリコンバレーの最前線で起きているリアルが生々しすぎ。

Googleが27億ドル（約4,000億円超）もの巨額を投じて呼び戻した伝説の研究者Noam Shazeer（Transformer論文の共著者）が、わずか2年足らずでライバルのOpenAIに移籍してしまった。

その理由が...

年収や役職の不満ではなく、「自分のチームのGPUの割り当てを削られたから」

4,000億円積んでも、計算リソースが足りなければ天才は一瞬で逃げてしまう。

いまトップ層のAIエンジニアにとって、GPUの割り当て枠は単なる会社のPCではなく酸素そのもの。どれだけ高い給料をもらっても、自分の仮説を高速で実験できない環境にいれば、研究者としての寿命が縮んでしまう。

記事によるとH100のレンタル価格は過去1年で約60%高騰し、かつて対立していたマスクとAnthropicすら水面下で計算資源を融通し合うほど、世界中で奪い合いが起きている。

なので現場の勝敗を真に分けているのは天才たちに何万枚のGPUを割り当てられるか、という泥臭い調達力と配分の決断だったりする。

text:
美国加州伯克利发生的一起同事投毒案，近日因一段监控视频曝光，再次引发关注。

现年50岁的女化学工程师 Rong Yuan 从2017年开始不断出现脱发、呕吐等症状，多次被送往医院急诊，甚至专程飞往中国求医，却始终找不到病因。直到2019年，她怀疑有人在自己的饮用水中动手脚，于是从亚马逊购买了一台隐蔽摄像头，安装在办公室。

监控画面显示，同事 David Xu 曾多次接近她的水瓶，其中2019年3月4日的视频清楚拍到他将某种物质倒入瓶中。警方调查发现，Xu 长期在她的食物和饮用水中投放有毒重金属镉，持续超过一年。检测显示，水瓶中的镉浓度最高竟达到美国联邦饮用水标准的350万倍。

2019年3月，Xu 被捕，被控谋杀未遂及两项重罪投毒罪，最高可能面临终身监禁。然而，检方后来与他达成认罪协议，撤销谋杀未遂及其中一项投毒指控。Xu 对剩余一项投毒罪选择不抗辩，2024年最终被判处两年缓刑，实际仅被关押一天。

今年3月，Xu 已完成缓刑，并进一步向法院申请撤销重罪定罪记录。

这也正是监控视频直到现在才公开的原因。 10月10日，受害者 Rong Yuan 首次公开讲述自己的遭遇，并主动向<旧金山标准报>等媒体提供了2019年拍摄的监控录像。

Rong Yuan 对当年的轻判结果极为不满。她表示，投毒至今仍给自己留下长期健康问题，导致她无法全职工作。她尤其担心，一旦 Xu 的撤销定罪申请获准，未来雇主可能无法通过普通背景调查查出他的犯罪记录。

10月12日，Xu 的撤销定罪申请安排在加州阿拉米达县高等法院审理，检方已对申请提出反对。Rong Yuan 希望通过公开视频，让社会重新关注这起案件。她说：“这个司法制度已经让我失望了，这是我最后的办法。”

text:
不得不说，Alexandr Wang 的做题底子的确很强，数学、物理、信息学三大学科竞赛都拿过国家级成绩，属于奥赛通才。

数学： 2013 年入选 Math Olympiad Program（MOP，这是美国数学奥林匹克集训、国家队选拔营）。
另有说法称，他在 2013 年 USAMO 中进入全美前 30 左右；不过 USAMO 本身不是排名赛，所谓前 30通常指高分段或 Honor Roll 一类名单。
此外，他还在 2012 年 USA Mathematical Talent Search 中获得全国第 5 名。

物理： 2014 年入选 US Physics Team。需要说明的是，美国物理队通常是约 20 人名单，之后从中选拔 5 人代表美国参加 IPhO，而不是一开始就只取最后 12 人。他的父母都是洛斯阿拉莫斯的物理学家，他从幼儿园起就被教物理，此等结果十分合理。

信息学： 2012、2013 年连续两年是 USACO 全国决赛选手，也受邀参加过集训营。USACO 决赛后，训练营中前 4 名代表美国参加 IOI；公开记录中，我没有查到他进入 IOI 国家队。 

他在访谈中谈过，自己在数学、计算机、物理三个方向都进入过美国国家级选拔或集训阶段，并说自己在不同阶段分别对数学、物理、编程高度专注。

由于美国国家队选拔营的体量比中国集训队小，选拔人群的深度也不同，整体来看，中国顶端的训练强度和人口基数更大，所以同样的入营，含金量通常略低于中国的集训队。
 
数学MOP + USAMO 前 30 左右，个人感觉大致相当于中国数学联赛一等奖里的偏上档，到 CMO 银牌中上至金牌下沿。不到国家集训队的稳定水平，更不是国家队 6 人。USAMO 本身一般认为比 CMO 略易，所以这个排名折算下来不算很高。
 
物理US Physics Team，约 20 人名单，对应的大约是CPhO决赛金牌到银牌上沿，接近国家集训队边缘。美国队约 20 人，之后再选 5 人出赛 IPhO。他的具体名次没有查到，这是三科里相对最强。
 
信息学USACO 决赛 + 集训营邀请，应该大致相当于 NOI 铜牌到银牌之间，或省队级别，距国家集训队有明显差距。2012–2013 年的 USACO 难度，和现在不能直接比。我做过相关题，当时整体明显比现在容易。

不过，三科同时进国家级选拔，在国内我认识的同学里几乎找不到完全对应的人。毕竟，国内高中生基本是单科冲刺，同时在三科达到省队以上的很少。单科深度上，我觉得他更接近省队or冬令营银牌的档次，并没有到集训队or国家队的档次。所以Alexandr Wang的奥赛通才含金量主要在广度。但即使如此，也足以证明其天资。

text:
这期播客里最扎心的一段细节，是聊到 Muse 是怎么被造出来的。

大家习惯了看硅谷神话，以为现象级产品的诞生靠的是某天夜里的灵光乍现。
Alexandr Wang 亲口承认：那个让人惊艳的原型，他们一两周就拉出来了，拿去给董事会做演示，台下掌声一片。
但为了把这个时灵时不灵的原型推向大众，他们整整按住没发，耗费了七个月。
在今天的 AI 圈子里，七个月漫长得就像过去了整整十年。

每天都有新模型在发推特，每周都有新的初创公司宣布颠覆世界，在那种全世界都在高喊快鱼吃慢鱼的狂躁氛围里，能把一个惊艳的产品按在实验室里一点一点打磨，需要极其可怕的战略克制。

Alex说了一句大实话：
在真实的消费级市场里，稳定可靠就是最好的产品，一旦偶尔会坏，在用户眼里它就是一堆垃圾。

很多人以为做出爆款靠的是第一次演示时的魔法感。

但工程的真相永远像砂纸一样粗粝：
把一百项日常行为逐行列成清单，忍着寂寞在那些没人看得见的边角死磕，把九次神奇一次崩溃的玩具，磨成十次里十次都能稳稳落地的工具。

原型展示的是天才的灵气，而能把灵气变成基础设施的，
从来只有那份对现实泥泞保持敬畏的枯燥体力。 https://t.co/KHAQ2iQdW6
author: AYi_AInotes
quoted_text:
晚上把 Meta首席AI官Alexandr Wang 和 David Senra 刚聊完的这 72 分钟完整看完了，
今年年初，整个 AI 圈的共识极其整齐划一：
Anthropic 在编程智能体上一骑绝尘，所有人都觉得会写代码的 Agent 才是唯一的大生意，无数资金和创业团队红着眼扑进代码补全和终端重构的泥潭里。

但 Meta 在那个节骨眼上，做了一个极其反直觉的掉头。

他们不去跟风卷程序员的饭碗，而是调集了不到两百人的精锐，关起门来死磕个人智能体。

这段决策逻辑让我回味了很久，甚至比任何算力竞赛都更清醒。

大家总以为最先进的生产力必须先替代复杂的智力劳动，却忘了商业最底层的地心引力：
全世界真正写代码的人只有几千万，但每天在手机屏幕前醒来、需要面对生活琐碎的普通人，足足有三十五亿。

扎克伯格其实看得很透，Meta 几十年积攒下来的血脉，从来不是冰冷的技术开发栈，而是人与人之间的连接、兴趣与好奇。

当其他实验室还在把智能体当成冷冰冰的数字工位时，他们已经在赌那张属于生活本身的底牌。

也许AGI 最动人的承诺，从来不是替你多敲几行代码，
而是我们终于可以不必再把一生最好的时光耗费在那些必须做的事情上，
我们也终于能把所有的呼吸与精力，完完整整地还给你真正想做的事。

Chris says DeFi is at its most vulnerable, pushing intermediaries to step in until policy and tech catch up

"There's no choice. You gotta use an intermediary. That's another lesson of this cycle. DeFi is beautiful. It's great. An incredible vision."

"But it's really hard to have a huge amount of assets like your personal wealth in DeFi if you're vulnerable. I'm hopeful that in the medium term, we'll have AI tools that help defend us."

"Many of us got into this space for the promise of decentralized finance, after spending years and years on Wall Street. We want that ideal."

"I've always ascertained that intermediaries should not be necessary, but they may be wanted. And unfortunately, now is the time you may want an intermediary, someone to safeguard your assets."

"It just feels like we're at max security vulnerability right now. And between the policy side and the tech side, I honestly believe it's gonna get cleaned up."

"The early days of the Internet were no different. You wouldn't in a million years put your credit card into the Internet back in the 90s when I was in college. It would be gone in 2 seconds."

"I do think tech will solve for it. But it does seem like we're in a period of max vulnerability. So intermediaries are stepping in to close those gaps."

10 remarks on AI and math that can be true all at once:
1. The recent progress is stunning and exciting.
2. The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis is arguably Fields-medal level.
3. Mathematics is being transformed and there is no way back.
4. OpenAI doesn't give a fuck about the future of mathematics.
5. Half-baked unreadable preprints claiming major results can effectively stall mathematical progress.
6. Some mathematicians are responding with naive, overly defensive comments.
7. The social-media wankers framing this as "OpenAI tramples gatekeeping" have no experience of mathematical research.
8. The product of mathematics is clarity and understanding. Not theorems, by themselves.
9. Mathematics is a critical infrastructure of human cognition. The human need for understanding isn't obsolete and it can't be offloaded to machines.
10. We haven't "solved" mathematics and we won't get there before the Sun burns out.

Last month, the contracts powering Magic Eden were exploited to the tune of millions of dollars. I was lucky enough to be in a position to rescue a good portion of that, but it highlighted the danger of leaving approvals open as adversaries get access to better and better tools for finding holes in contract logic. 

Today, Blur announced that they will be deprecating their frontend. 

I've investigated Blur and found no exploits within the current contracts. However, the Blur contracts are upgradable, meaning that they could turn malicious at any time.

They currently have eight figures worth of NFTs approved to them. The safety of those NFTs effectively hinges on the opssec of the Blur team, which appears to be disbanding at this time. 

If you have open approvals to Blur, I recommend you remove them immediately. Use https://t.co/3zfwoDIeZV  or similar to ensure that you are protected in case of a contract exploit or later upgrade.

Don't wait. The time is now.

author: sreeramkannan
quoted_text:
Mike was my colleague at Berkeley, and he's been fairly skeptical of deep learning's trajectory for years. Most scientists are skeptics, and it can take a big shock to get someone to consider a possibility that goes against the anchoring effect coded in our DNA.

I too was somewhat of a skeptic until ~6 months ago, and people ask me all the time why I joined Anthropic. 

It started in April, when a friend I've known for 20 yrs messaged me saying he'd be in the Bay Area in a week, and he suggested we meet up. I invited him to my house for dinner, and he told me he had just joined Anthropic. He said the models were becoming increasingly more capable, and he believed both that they'd soon be smarter than him and also that all intellectual work would be highly devalued in the near future, and lastly that society was not at all ready for what's coming.

I'd of course heard claims similar to this before, but not from a friend I'd known for this long, and who I trusted, at my dining room table. It was the initial shock needed to destabilize my own anchoring. Also, I've been fortunate to work with and/or mentor many smart people in my life (e.g. Fields medalists, a 4x Putnam Fellow, IOI first place winners, etc.), so I feel pretty calibrated in recognizing very smart people, and this was someone who is definitely very smart and with impressive such credentials. So, it was hard to ignore this friend saying the models would be smarter than even him in particular.

After that dinner, I decided to do an informal survey, calling and meeting up with a lot of my friends who now work on improving model capabilities at these frontier labs. They all agreed with that first friend. These were all people I'd known 10, 15, 20 years, who mentored me, or I mentored them, or we met professionally in academia. These are people I trust, and their beliefs on this topic were consistent.

I then spent a whole lot of time understanding the missions of different companies, and talking to current and former employees and people in leadership. I read Dario's (long) essays and watched videos on YouTube of company leaders being interviewed. Anthropic's stated mission "to ensure that the world safely makes the transition through transformative AI" felt like exactly the right guiding principle to handle such a society-disrupting technology, and everyone I spoke to at the company was very aligned with this mission. It's easily the most mission-focused place I've ever been at, and everyone takes the work extremely seriously and with a profound sense of responsibility.

And now here I am. And being on the inside, the pace of progress has surprised me more than I first imagined. The moment that pure mathematicians are in, to me, is just a microcosm of what I predict a much larger of society will be grappling with in the not too distant future, and I really hope our leaders and the general public internalize sooner than later just how significant a moment we're in.

author: bigironchris
quoted_text:
FAST⚡️ when fast is enough. Slower only when it takes that to get it 🧠 RIGHT.

What we learned selling decision models to corporates:

- Everyone loves low latency, but in many cases being right matters more. Customers don’t know (or care) whether a question is System 1 or System 2. They’ll happily wait a few hundred extra ms for the right answer.

- That’s why @LevantoLabs pioneered reasoning for decision models. Sage answers easy questions in ~100 ms, detects when a question is harder, and reasons only then.

- Soon every decision model will expose a latency–accuracy dial. Glide and TypeLLM have already implemented "reasoning". More will come.
